## Media Pod Team Structure
Use when: You are structuring (or restructuring) the in-house team that produces and runs your store's paid and organic content.
- Form pods of two: one analytical/briefing person who handles meetings, data, and posting, and one creative person who shoots and edits.
- Enforce the strict rule that the creative person does not attend meetings or fill out spreadsheets.
- Give each pod autonomy over its own creative output as long as results are measurable.
- Merge media buying and organic strategy responsibilities where practical — the source frames this convergence as the direction of the role.
- Evolve the senior marketing role toward a tactical head of content rather than a meeting-heavy director.
Caveat: Pod design suits content-heavy marketing; not every store has the volume to justify it.
Caveat: Source describes this as an organizational model, not a proven org chart for all businesses.

Tags: multi, operations, team-structure, media-pods, creative-enablement
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Eliminating Bureaucratic Creative Review
Use when: Creative approvals for ads or product pages are slow because many stakeholders weigh in.
- Audit creative review meetings: if the outcome can be swayed by politics rather than measurable KPIs — the source's example is 13 people debating a social post — cancel the meeting.
- Remove non-essential stakeholders from the review so the decision belongs to the people accountable for the number.
- Apply the enablement rule: the person doing the work owns the decision as long as it is measurable (e.g., the designer choosing a button color).
- Set a measurable success metric before the decision so review is about the data afterward, not opinions beforehand.
Caveat: Removing review reduces coordination but can allow off-brand or off-strategy creative; keep brand guardrails separate from performance review.
Caveat: The source frames this as an operating principle for fast-moving teams.

Tags: multi, operations, creative-enablement, process-design, decision-making
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Trend Execution SLAs with Pre-Approved Budget
Use when: A trend is moving fast and your normal approval chain would make the content too late to matter.
- Set a pre-approved budget ceiling for trend-based creative — the source cites an example of $1,200.
- Set a strict execution timeline — the source cites an example of 36 hours — for external creators to produce and ship.
- Remove leadership sign-off from within that window so the creator can act immediately.
- Review the spend and performance after the fact rather than gating it beforehand.
Caveat: The $1,200 and 36-hour figures are the source's examples; calibrate to your own margins, creator rates, and risk tolerance.
Caveat: Pre-approved budgets require trust and a clear scope so spend doesn't drift.

Tags: multi, operations, trend-marketing, creator-management, process-design, budgeting
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Zero-budget store launch: free organic video first, then $10/day Meta validation
Use when: Product selection, launch strategy, or acquisition planning for a new store or brand with a tiny or zero marketing budget.
- Treat organic social video as a free attention channel: post short videos or carousels on TikTok/Instagram/Reels. The source's claim is that any post gets at least a few hundred views from the start, and good ones get far more — so even the smallest brand can compete for attention without ad spend.
- Produce a high volume of cheap creative (the source's example: try on the order of 50 social videos made for free) rather than perfecting a small set of launch assets.
- Read organic performance to find outlier creative — the pieces that clearly beat your own baseline (source example: average 800 views, one piece hits 4,000+).
- Take validated organic winners and load them into Meta ads, starting near $10/day. Use roughly $300 total to validate a product, whether software, info product, or physical product.
- Use the same account structure for testing: a test campaign at roughly $10–$50/day with 1–3 new creative pieces added every few days, separate from a scale campaign.
- Double budgets on winners stepwise (e.g., $50 → $100 → $200/day) and watch for diminishing returns; when returns drop, decide whether the constraint is more creative or product interest.
Caveat: The minimum-views and budget figures are the source's examples, not guaranteed benchmarks; validate your own baseline.
Caveat: Small budgets mean slow validation — a $150 product at $10/day can take weeks to read.
Caveat: The 'double it' scaling approach breaks down at high spend levels and is only suggested for small-scale testing.

Tags: multi, acquisition, creative-strategy, budgeting, meta-ads, organic-social
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Diagnose ad creative by two signals: does it get spend, and does it return money?
Use when: Interpreting early Meta ad results to decide whether to kill, fix, or scale a piece of creative.
- Run each creative in a test campaign at low daily spend ($10–$50) with a few new pieces added every few days.
- Check signal one — does Meta give it spend? Meta allocates spend when people engage, like, or watch the creative and a demographic can be found. No spend means no one is interested; retire it.
- Check signal two — does it convert? If it gets spend but no money back, the source says the likely cause is the ad or landing page failing to give enough info, context, or link between ad and page. Fix the message or the page.
- If it gets spend and returns money, raise the budget (double it at small scale) and keep adding new creative alongside it.
- Expect low-spend tests to take days to weeks; treat the read as a numbers game and track it diligently.
Caveat: The $10–$50/day range and 'double it' rule are the source's small-business examples, not universal ad rules.
Caveat: Meta's delivery behavior and campaign interfaces change; verify current ad-manager setup before relying on this structure.

Tags: multi, meta-ads, creative-strategy, experiment-design, measurement, acquisition
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Build an empathy avatar feed to escape founder-centric content
Use when: Content and creative planning when content feels about the founder rather than the customer, or when a brand lacks customer understanding.
- Define one or two customer avatars (e.g., younger guys who want to bulk up for a fitness product).
- Create a separate Twitter/Instagram/TikTok account and follow the people your avatar follows — look at who they follow and replicate that feed.
- Review that dummy feed and ask: what content are they normally digesting, what do they want to get out of it (laugh, cry, get info, meet people), and what time of day do they engage?
- Use those answers to shape content angle, tone, and format before writing anything.
- Apply a self-check reminder before publishing: 'no one cares about your story, they care about the value you give them.' A story can be about you only if it has value, interest, or entertainment for the avatar.
- Optional source tactic: use a phone app that requires you to state why you're opening social media, reinforcing the customer-serving mindset.
Caveat: The source frames 'I'm not creative' as a fallacy — the working substitute is empathy with the customer, not artistic talent.
Caveat: This is a diagnostic and framing habit, not a guarantee of reach or conversion.

Tags: multi, customer-research, creative-strategy, content, positioning, organic-social
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Separate analytical and creative roles in a media pod
Use when: Designing or reorganizing a marketing team so creative output isn't bottlenecked by meetings and admin.
- Pair one analytical/briefing person (handles meetings, data, posting, priorities) with one creative/creator (shoots, edits, or is on camera).
- Enforce the rule: the creative person does not attend meetings or fill out spreadsheets — their job is to get creative done.
- Give the analyst responsibility for keeping the creator's calendar full, reporting in, and adjusting priorities.
- Expand by pod: e.g., creator + creator + social manager + editor as one pod; designers + strategist as another; decide whether paid media can ride on one person who also does analytics.
- At roughly a 10-person team, run it like a writer's room: surface all ideas and product-marketing input, stress-test them, then distribute into an asset flow feeding paid and organic.
- Consider merging organic and paid teams so the same faces go back and forth on every decision.
Caveat: The source's structural claims (roles being absorbed, director-of-marketing equals social manager) are their opinion about a trend, not a fixed org chart.
Caveat: Team size and pod composition depend on volume and budget; the 10-person writer's-room example is illustrative.

Tags: multi, team-design, operations, creative-strategy, process
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Cancel creative reviews that can be swayed by politics
Use when: Fixing slow or politically-driven creative approval processes in a store's marketing workflow.
- Identify review meetings where many stakeholders debate a single creative asset (the source's example: 13 people debating a social post). If the decision hinges on taste rather than a KPI, cancel the meeting.
- Assign ownership of measurable creative choices to the person doing the work — e.g., the UX designer choosing a button color owns that decision as long as it is measurable.
- Set pre-approved budgets and timelines for fast trend execution: the source's example is a $1,200 budget and a 36-hour window for external creators to execute on a social trend without leadership sign-off.
- Remove non-essential stakeholders from creative reviews to eliminate the 'expensive meeting' where cost far exceeds the decision's value.
Caveat: The $1,200 budget and 36-hour SLA are the source's examples, not universal thresholds; set yours by decision stakes.
Caveat: The source's stance against cross-departmental review is an opinion; high-risk brand or compliance decisions may still need sign-off outside this rule.

Tags: multi, process, operations, creative-strategy, team-design
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Let organic viral hooks become paid ad assets
Use when: Converting organic social performance into paid acquisition creative for a store.
- Post organic content aimed at your avatar's problems and goals; watch for outliers above your own baseline.
- Option one — take the entire piece that popped, including its organic comments, and load it into the ad account as-is (the source notes you can use an ad code and whitelist it if it's on a team member's account).
- Option two — if only the hook resonated, reuse that hook and rework the body into a product promo. Source example: a gym owner's viral video about 1980s Kentucky strength training didn't help the gym, but using that hook and then promoting how the gym applies those principles produced a usable ad.
- Check whether the winning piece even mentions the product; if not, decide between running it for awareness/attention or rebuilding it into a product-linked ad.
- At a from-scratch level, the source's simple rule is: whatever concept got a few thousand views organically, put that into the ad account.
Caveat: The source says this simple 'just put it in the ad account' approach is for zero-to-one stage; brand building at higher levels is more nuanced.
Caveat: High views with negative sentiment is a different signal — the source says it mostly occurs with off-the-wall content, not straightforward content.

Tags: multi, creative-strategy, meta-ads, organic-social, content, acquisition
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Skip the founder on camera — use an expert or friendly face
Use when: Deciding who appears in a store's on-camera content when the founder won't or can't record.
- Reject the assumption that content must be the founder or CEO — the source calls that a fallacy.
- Prioritize an expert in the niche: the source cites getting a dermatologist, nurse, or someone in scrubs or a hat who believes in the product and sits on the advisory board. Expert credibility can outperform founder credibility.
- If no true expert is available, use a personable, friendly person (a model, an employee, a hired creator) reading a script written by a professional — the source says this gets the same job done.
- Match the type of story to the person: a founder tells certain stories, an expert tells others.
- Budget for it: pay the expert a budget or equity if they genuinely believe in the product and give real advice, then trickle content down from there.
Caveat: The expert-credibility advantage is the source's opinion; results depend on category and audience.
Caveat: For regulated categories (the source mentions medical, peptides, wellness) check applicable advertising and endorsement rules before using practitioner claims.

Tags: multi, content, creative-strategy, organic-social, influencer
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Break the brand-account rule: run separate accounts for content-market fit
Use when: Organic acquisition strategy when the brand account is struggling to earn attention or the product can't carry content on its own.
- Recognize that people follow people, not companies (source example: audiences follow founders like Gary Vee, not the agency brand).
- Consider a fully separate account — the source cites Opal, which ran a whiteboard-tutorial account about mental health with plugs for the app at the end, on an account without a related handle.
- Build valuable or entertaining content for the target demographic first, and solve content-market fit before integrating the product heavily.
- Choose whatever format fits: a person, a separate persona account, a clips account, an aggregator, or the brand account — the source says it doesn't matter.
- Only later fold the product in more strongly once the audience and content formula are validated.
- Treat brand risk as a risk-reward tradeoff: the source argues over-weighting brand risk is itself the biggest threat to brand success in a fast-moving environment.
Caveat: Running content without a brand handle is the source's strategic advice and its brand-risk tradeoff position, not a guaranteed outcome.
Caveat: Platform rules on undisclosed paid promotion and accounts impersonating or misrepresenting brands may apply — check current policies.

Tags: multi, organic-social, creative-strategy, acquisition, content, positioning
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Diagnose spend-stage measurability loss and bet on one awareness initiative
Use when: Marketing planning for a store spending roughly six figures a month, where clean ROI tracking has stopped working.
- Recognize the transition: at low spend, track return on ad spend and returns from organic; a marketing efficiency ratio (spend vs. revenue) works well when you're doing only a few things.
- Expect that tracking to break somewhere around the mid-tens-of-millions in revenue / 8–20% of revenue on marketing — the source's rough heuristic, after which scaling with that measurability stalls for most brands.
- Move into the intangible: generate brand awareness and activities that let you scale spend further, even though the math gets fuzzier.
- Pick one new initiative to be best at, not three or four — the source says trying multiple is impossible. Source examples: a cosmetics brand building a large Snapchat following when no competitor was there; a cosmetics brand going all in on influencer trips for their ripple and viral effects.
- Plan properly when the initiative requires it (e.g., an influencer trip needs about four months of lead time) rather than insisting on a one-week cycle.
- When the bet works, ask 'how many of these can we do?' and hit it as fast as possible — the source argues fatigue is no longer the limiting factor; gaps in the internet are.
Caveat: The revenue bands (roughly $20–50M, 8–20% of revenue on marketing, tracking breaking in that range) are source-specific heuristics, not a formula.
Caveat: Some brands do keep scaling with measurability — the source says 'most can't,' not all.
Caveat: This stage still requires fiscal discipline on content and ads, not abandoning measurement.

Tags: multi, budgeting, measurement, brand-awareness, acquisition, strategy
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Build customer personas from real purchase data, not assumptions
Use when: Customer research and audience targeting for a store that already has a customer list and wants reliable segments.
- Stop relying on tiny surveys or executive guesses — the source calls out personas built from 8 customers or the CMO's opinion as unreliable.
- Run the customer email database and ecommerce customer list through a data platform (the source names Outer Signal) to generate data-derived personas (e.g., 30–35-year-old drivers in urban areas who also buy certain things).
- Use the resulting personas — the source says you may get several, and you can document and pin them up as reference.
- Apply the same tooling to identify customers who are also influencers or creators; the source cites a women's wear brand where about one in eight customers was an influencer, previously found by manually Googling each customer.
- Take the top 10% most interesting or influential customers and contact them directly — even if that's the marketing team — to seed product, get feedback, learn about their experience, and ask for content.
Caveat: Outer Signal is named by the source as the tool used; verify current features and pricing before adopting.
Caveat: Results depend on data quality and list size; personas from a small customer base will be weaker.

Tags: multi, customer-research, retention, influencer, measurement, segmentation
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Turn existing customers into the content flywheel
Use when: Building a retention and content engine for a store using its own customer base rather than paid creators.
- Run your customer base through a data platform to surface high-value or notable customers (the source's Whisper Flow example: a customer who turned out to be Steven Bartlett posted 630K-view content).
- Email or DM those customers personally: thank them, start a relationship, then ask whether they'd do a testimonial, whether you can pay them for something, or whether you can run their existing post as a whitelisted ad.
- Look for customers who already posted about the product unprompted; asking to run and edit their genuine content often beats brand-made creative (source example: a creator who loved a chair and a game console was asked to let the brand edit their videos into ads).
- Prioritize the top 10% most influential customers for direct contact; automate or skip the long tail if bandwidth is limited.
- Extend the same approach to your broader audience, including notable followers — the source mentions a team system for tracking who's hot in a following and who to message.
- Keep it human: message people like a friend (a funny reel, something that made you think of them), not a mass promotional email that reads as spam.
Caveat: This approach takes manual time; the source warns that a fully AI-automated version 'defeats the point' of real human relationships.
Caveat: Disclose paid partnerships and secure creator permission before running their content as ads per current platform rules.

Tags: multi, retention, customer-research, creative-strategy, influencer, community
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Anchor advocacy on product experience, then add value and entertainment
Use when: Retention and brand-building planning for a store that wants customers to actively root for the brand, not just buy.
- Start with the product: does it make the customer's life significantly better? Advocacy follows a superior product experience; the source's example is a mic-replacement app recommended purely because it improved someone's life, with zero knowledge of its social presence.
- Once product experience is right, decide what value or entertainment you provide online — the source's two levers.
- Deliver genuine value, e.g., a fitness product bundling free workouts or classes the customer would have paid for.
- Or deliver entertainment, e.g., a jewelry brand running an ongoing series/show with characters and a narrative that fans follow.
- Then think like a TV network: inventory all your events, contributors (influencers, customers, team), and world happenings, and shape them into a bigger narrative.
- Treat radical customer service and experience as a differentiator, especially when competitors are automating it away — the source flags this as a stand-out opportunity.
Caveat: Product experience is the source's stated prerequisite; branding alone cannot manufacture advocacy from a flawed product.
Caveat: The Alexis Bittar and Whisper Flow examples are illustrations, not evidence of a repeatable benchmark.

Tags: multi, retention, brand-awareness, community, customer-research, content
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Use a wheelhouse setting — a garage, workshop, or warehouse — as a content stage
Use when: Organic content planning for a store with a physical workspace or hands-on process that can be filmed.
- Identify a real, credible space — the source mentions garages, workshops, warehouses, or manufacturing floors. It 'doesn't have to be glamorous.'
- Put a character from that environment on camera. Source example: a Porsche restoration shop where the mechanic explains what he's fixing, model-year problems, and the four replacement options he considered and which he chose.
- Plan content as a funnel: top-of-funnel pieces where the character says something provocative or culturally current to get views (may not sell, but builds awareness); middle-of-funnel educational content (e.g., how a product line came together) that gets fewer views but nurtures.
- Put the same face into your paid ads — the source calls out brands that run great live-selling talent but never put those people on the main feed or in ads.
- Let the character become a recognizable brand asset customers follow and route attention back to the product over time.
Caveat: The source says all content is a funnel, but top-of-funnel provocation may not convert — it's awareness, not sales.
Caveat: Characters and their on-camera behavior carry brand risk; the source treats that risk as an acceptable tradeoff, which you should weigh yourself.

Tags: multi, content, creative-strategy, organic-social, brand-awareness, production
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Build a funnel-weighted content mix for organic and paid
Use when: Planning the monthly content calendar and creative pipeline for a store's organic channels and paid ad account.
- Classify every planned piece as top-of-funnel (broad, viral, tribal, opinion-bait) or mid-funnel (educational, how-it's-made, tactical).
- Pick your mix based on current reach: if you post ~5x/week and have low reach, run roughly 2 top-of-funnel to 3 mid-funnel; if you already have strong reach on most posts, flip to 1 or 0 top-of-funnel and focus mid/bottom.
- Use top-of-funnel to widen TAM and trigger the platform's 'show more of this account' behavior; use mid-funnel to convert that wider audience into fans and buyers.
- Put the same people who appear in lives or organic content into the main feed and the paid ads — the source notes a sunscreen brand whose strong live hosts were absent from feed and ads, wasting existing affinity.
- Extend the same faces to bottom-of-funnel ads and whitelisting so new audiences see a recognizable person rather than a faceless ad.
Caveat: The 2:3 split is the source's heuristic for a posting 5x/week, not a measured benchmark.
Caveat: This is the presenter's opinion on how social feeds reward content, not a guaranteed algorithmic rule.

Tags: multi, content-strategy, creative-strategy, acquisition, awareness, paid-ads, organic-social
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Use versus formats and qualifiers to trigger tribal engagement
Use when: Writing hooks and formats for top-of-funnel social or ad creative that needs to reach beyond your existing buyers.
- Use a versus format: compare two things and take a clear 'good/bad' stance so viewers form an opinion (e.g., a dentist listing which dental products are bad for you).
- Layer a qualifier into the hook to niche it down and make a subgroup self-identify — e.g., 'best dental floss for wife guys' or 'introverts need an extroverted spouse'.
- Alternatively open a curiosity gap (viewers stay to see the final result or fit) or make a tribal-belief claim (e.g., 'maximalism beats minimalism').
- Map your ideas to one of five broad tribal pillars (wealth, health, relationships, politics, religion) or a subcategory within it (parenting, dating, luxury, etc.), since the source says every viral video it has made sat in one of these.
- Avoid attaching your brand to pillars that clash with it — the source deliberately avoids politics for its own content even though it drives virality.
Caveat: Tribal pillars are the source's observation from its own content, not a validated universal taxonomy.
Caveat: Politically/religiously charged angles can drive views but risk brand damage; treat as situational.

Tags: multi, content-strategy, hooks, creative-strategy, acquisition, positioning
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Inject brand personality overtly and covertly
Use when: Making a store's brand content feel distinct instead of generic, especially when formats are being copied from competitors.
- Covert signals: control the background, set, wardrobe and props so viewers infer the brand's world (the source's YouTube set with medieval helmets, streetwear wardrobe as a signal of a niche).
- Overt signals: let on-camera people talk about real life — being a dad, a hobby, a specific lived experience — kept anecdotal rather than scripted.
- Add an expertise frame at the start of a copied format: instead of 'things in Paris I find chic', say 'things in Paris I find chic as a first-year interior design student'.
- Once you have a format that already performs, append a 'video within a video' — a short personal tangent or second mini-story — to introduce personality without changing the working format.
- Make at least one joke per video; the source's own standard is roughly one joke per video, though humor won't land with everyone.
Caveat: Source's own practice, not a tested causal driver of sales.
Caveat: Personality without an interesting underlying concept still won't perform — the source stresses the initial concept must be interesting or made interesting.

Tags: multi, content-strategy, brand-voice, creative-strategy, organic-social
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Establish proven formats before trend-jacking
Use when: Deciding whether to chase a trending sound/format for a store's social channels.
- First build formats unique (or unique enough) to your brand that you've tested into; hopping on trends with no working strategy in place won't fix underperforming social.
- Once formats work, build a trend response path: identify a fast-turnaround creator and pre-agree a rate, e.g. delivery back in ~36 hours for a set fee.
- Pre-approve the budget so a marketing lead can greenlight a trend spend without new approvals — the source cites ~$1,200 as an example pre-approved amount.
- Run a quick internal signal (meeting or shared Slack) where the team asks 'should we go?' and answers yes/no against known cost — cosmetics trends were described as done within ~72 hours, so speed is the constraint.
- Decide in advance which regular work gets deprioritized when a trend fires.
Caveat: The 36-hour and 72-hour figures and $1,200 budget are examples from the source's clients, not universal benchmarks.
Caveat: Trend clock speed varies by category; verify current platform/vendor workflows.

Tags: multi, content-strategy, trends, creative-strategy, operations, organic-social
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Match trend timing to where your customer sits on the bell curve
Use when: Choosing how fast your store should adopt trends versus letting them pass.
- Map your customer: ultra-trendy customers require you to be the trend setter or one step behind; customers who lag the curve can safely adopt a trend weeks later.
- Example from the source: Aritzia ran viral TSA-bin style content around Black Friday, roughly six months after it peaked, and it still worked because its working-women customer was behind the curve and saw it as new.
- Example: an iPhone case brand was described as consistently one degree behind visual trends, shooting weekly or biweekly — 'level two' trendy but not a setter.
- For brands selling to late adopters, treat a late trend as free, pre-validated creative rather than something to avoid.
- Tie the decision to the customer persona exercise rather than to what your competitors are doing.
Caveat: Bell-curve positioning is a framework, not a measured segmentation; the Aritzia and case-brand examples are illustrative.
Caveat: Being late on a fast-decaying trend in a trend-driven category can read as stale.

Tags: multi, trends, customer-research, content-strategy, positioning
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Prioritize volume of creator content and a network of faces
Use when: Allocating creator/influencer budget and building a store's content supply.
- Default to a volume strategy: the source describes large programs seeding thousands of creators per month with seeding packs, achieving roughly 50%+ post rates on one project.
- Anchor with one big creator only if it kickstarts excitement, then immediately layer in many smaller creators ('add the 60... then the next 60').
- Build a network of 5-6 (or more) faces who each serve a different target demographic or region — the source cites a surf brand using ~8-10 people covering markets like Australia, viral stunt content and tutorials.
- Use each face for what they're good at: viral moments, tutorials, education, regional credibility; coordinate via a shared channel asking what each is making and where collabs fit.
- Accept that finding many creators is 10x the work of contracting one — that workload is the tradeoff for better results.
Caveat: The ~50% post rate and 'thousands per month' are project-specific examples, not benchmarks.
Caveat: Volume programs require real ops capacity; small teams may not sustain this.

Tags: multi, influencer-marketing, creative-strategy, acquisition, operations, content-strategy
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Design a two-tier brief system so creators can create
Use when: Writing marketing briefs for influencers/UGC creators and setting approval workflow at a store.
- Create a standard tier: content that must run through legal and full brand review.
- Create a second tier with wider allowed topics and no legal review, bounded by a small explicit no-go list (the source cites three prohibited topics as an example).
- Decide which campaigns or creators live inside the second tier and tell them upfront where the goalposts are.
- Keep the primary tier's rules minimal and specific; the source blames restrictive, corny briefs from big agencies for poor creator output.
- If briefs are consistently missing, bring in a creator/influencer as adviser — either an existing creator you work with or an agency that is actually tapped into content — to sanity-check briefs before they go out.
- If briefs are working and no one complains, the source says you don't need an adviser.
Caveat: This is a workflow recommendation from the source, not a tested program design.
Caveat: Compliance/legal requirements vary by category and jurisdiction; verify what can legally bypass review.

Tags: multi, influencer-marketing, brief-writing, operations, compliance, retention
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Use targeted creator metrics: saves, shares and intent, not just views
Use when: Setting KPIs and reporting for creator/influencer campaigns that aren't directly attributable to sales.
- Classify each creator as broad (job is views to a tangential-or-core audience at an acceptable CPM with more affinity than an ad) or targeted (job is reaching a specific persona).
- For broad creators, track view volume and CPM against paid ad alternatives.
- For targeted creators, weight saves, shares and intent signals — the source cites a video about Amazon FBA changes with ~300 saves as ~300 people with genuine intent, valued against what those people are worth as leads.
- Do not judge awareness-focused creator work purely on directly attributable sales; the source calls that an 'old school' framing.
- Consider the four levels of influence: core influencers (directly measurable), new-market influencers (lower ROI, new audience), message/talent-aura plays (Super Bowl-style work aimed at peers/recruiters/agencies), and moonshot bets.
Caveat: Saves/share thresholds are the source's illustrative example, not a benchmark.
Caveat: Attribution for awareness spend remains genuinely hard; don't treat intent proxies as purchase conversion.

Tags: multi, measurement, influencer-marketing, awareness, acquisition, metrics
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Repurpose a winning asset across every distribution surface
Use when: Extending the life of a top-performing creator or organic asset across a store's channels.
- Check rights: confirm you can use the asset on your own channels and in paid before pushing it broadly.
- Push the same asset to every relevant platform — TikTok, LinkedIn, Snapchat, email and landing pages; encourage active employees to post organic/influencer content on LinkedIn for B2B reach.
- Produce localizations and look variants of a winning script: the source's example was English and Spanish voiceovers of the same first-person gameplay content, where the Spanish account outperformed the US account due to less competition.
- Segmented-email version: match the creator who appeals to a persona with the email segment for that persona.
- Broadcast winning videos to your creator/Discord/WhatsApp network so others replicate them — especially creators who look or sound different — until the concept stops generating results.
Caveat: Rights and whitelisting terms must be negotiated per creator; don't assume paid usage.
Caveat: Language/look variants require creators or tools you actually have access to.

Tags: multi, distribution, content-strategy, influencer-marketing, email, localization
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Use under-action tutorials instead of talking-head product demos
Use when: Producing product tutorials, demo videos and ad creative for a SKU.
- Shoot the tutorial in the middle of the activity the product is for — firing gel blasters mid-game, explaining a wake foil while riding it — rather than seated in front of the product.
- Keep the explanation running while the action happens, often with a live mic or voiceover.
- Add a benign tension variable: someone calm while doing something risky, or a supplement testimonial delivered between sets.
- Substitute the frame for your category: talking about a tire while standing in front of a car is generic; talking about the tire while driving at speed conveys the product's point.
- Test variants of the same script in this format in the ad account before scaling.
Caveat: Source's own preferred format, based on its client work — not measured across categories.
Caveat: Requires safe conditions; don't stage genuinely dangerous demonstrations.

Tags: multi, creative-strategy, product-page, demo-video, paid-ads, ugc
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Decide if you need a face — not necessarily the founder
Use when: Deciding who appears on camera in a store's organic and paid creative.
- Prioritize having consistent faces attached to the brand to build affinity and reach, regardless of whose faces they are.
- Recruit credible influencers/creators in your niche rather than defaulting to the founder; the source notes founders can become a liability as stakes rise (its phrasing: 'the more successful you get, the more likely your founder is a psycho').
- Do not over-invest in a single face; the source prefers a roster of 5-6 representing different demographics, with one big face as optional anchor only if the person is a perfect fit.
- For broad-TAM categories (brownies, water, mass consumer products), consider content watchable with no voiceover or language dependence because the addressable market is bigger.
- For intellectual/specialist products, use language and expertise deliberately, since no-voiceover content would not carry the same appeal.
Caveat: Founder-on-camera is a situational choice, not universally bad; the source's remark is a strong opinion.
Caveat: Creator roster cost and contract complexity scale with count.

Tags: multi, brand-voice, influencer-marketing, creative-strategy, positioning
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Kill decision-by-committee and tie creative choices to measurable owners
Use when: Fixing slow approval on conversion-relevant choices like button color, PDP layout or campaign creative.
- Ask of any review meeting: do the attendees have a genuine, informed opinion on this, and can the outcome be measured at a lower level?
- If yes — e.g. a button color on the success page of a checkout flow — let the UX designer own it, give them a KPI around conversion rate, and measure.
- If the choice can't be measured but is genuinely creative, let the designated content owners decide and bring quantifiable data monthly/weekly (e.g., pillar performance and analytics) for the team to respond to.
- Remove people without a basis in the work from creative review; the source describes 13-person creative reviews where a strong personality or lobbying group hijacks the creative.
- Cap meetings aggressively and adopt idea-murder-boarding: everyone posts all references, debate openly, and once a call is made to kill something, stop discussing it.
- Categorize review meetings: run as many as you like when attendees have real opinions and aren't swayed by politics; if not, just let it ship.
Caveat: Source's operating philosophy, not a studied org design.
Caveat: Small teams may not have specialized owners; the principle is to name accountability, not necessarily to hire.

Tags: multi, operations, conversion-optimization, experiment-design, product-page, checkout
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Budget meetings in people-cost and push toward bias for action
Use when: Diagnosing slow marketing operations at a store and reallocating team time to output.
- Estimate a meeting's cost by summing attendees' hourly cost multiplied by the meeting length plus the opportunity cost — the source refers to a recurring '~$50,000 meeting' in a Fortune 500 context.
- Replace low-value meetings with the work being deferred: sourcing new creators, briefing new creative, presenting data.
- Set a required flow: each person presents specific metrics/results to their manager on a weekly cadence, and managers present upward, with people actually reading and responding.
- Judge whether a meeting has a political outcome at stake; if so, only run it with people who own the decision, otherwise tolerate mistakes.
- Use the rule 'decisions that can be made with data or measured afterward belong to whoever does the work' as the default.
Caveat: The $50,000 figure is the source's illustration of meeting cost, not a general benchmark.
Caveat: Weekly metric-sharing pace suits growing teams; smaller teams may run leaner.

Tags: multi, operations, teamwork, measurement, reporting
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Preserve your marketing edge as the org grows
Use when: Scaling a store's marketing team past roughly seven figures a month in spend while keeping channel effectiveness.
- Check incoming hires' tolerance for the 'unemployed-level' tooling upkeep — the source claims keeping up with AI marketing tools suits people with time, not busy full-time teams.
- Protect edge via mandate, not goodwill: one PE-firm example required staff to document AI processes, which built reusable assets (e.g., brand-voice projects queryable by the whole org).
- Democratize across channels rather than relying on one — the source cites a brand running TikTok Shop, seeding, paid and big campaigns methodically at once.
- Recognize the structural gap: CMOs/VPs can become disconnected from execution while director-level roles carry the tactical load, so expect turnover and build around it.
- Adopt a writer's-room model for scaling creative: few calls, idea-murder-boarding, then put out.
Caveat: The PE and brand examples are illustrative and not from ecommerce benchmarking.
Caveat: The 'subject to keep up with AI tools is for the unemployed' line is a strong opinion from the source.

Tags: multi, operations, teamwork, ai-tools, creative-strategy, scaling
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Use staged adoption of AI for landing pages, copy and briefing
Use when: Deciding what AI workflows to deploy in a store's marketing and where to hold back.
- Adopt immediately: AI for generating copy, drafting landing pages and end-to-end LP generation — the source cites creators building full LPs from Claude.
- Adopt immediately: AI briefing/social-audit tooling that builds video databases with hook analysis and outlier detection to cut briefing time dramatically.
- Defer: AI-generated people/personas as influencers; the source says AI creators may perform in ad accounts but won't substitute for real creators in real settings.
- Defer: AI-generated visual content — fake luxury collab visuals can pass as real once reposted by aggregator accounts, but source cautions it looks bad and isn't worth the risk until output quality improves (its suggested window: wait until later in the year).
- Before running AI visual content, test whether customer hate actually touches revenue or subscribers; the source notes some brands got ~1,000 bad comments with no impact on revenue or subscribers, then decides based on willingness to absorb social flak.
Caveat: AI tool capability and platform policies change fast — verify current interfaces and rules before deploying.
Caveat: The 'wait a year' window is the source's opinion; not a validated timeline.
Caveat: Regulatory and disclosure rules around AI content vary by market.

Tags: multi, ai-tools, landing-page, copywriting, creative-strategy, operations
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Build creative in a limited set of repeatable systems, not by copying one trend
Use when: Planning a store's organic and paid creative pipeline for the next quarter.
- Confirm a format is working before scaling it — the source defines a working format as one whose variants you can spin up predictably.
- Once a winner exists, multiply it by audience dimension: language (e.g., English and Spanish voiceovers of the same shoot), look and demographic (skin tone, age, condition) to cover more of the TAM.
- For team practice: treat social like a writer's room with a pillar system and monthly analytics, letting an accountable person post what they want within the pillar framework.
- At scale, split 'core social' from 'special projects': the source says brands are adding heads by network (a Twitch person, a Twitter person) rather than one head of social.
- Keep the number of approvals thin, especially for creative review — source describes 'spitfire' teams where essentially one person reviews.
Caveat: Roles lists ('head of Twitter', etc.) reflect the source's observation, not a universal org template.
Caveat: Variant multiplication on top of a dead concept doesn't resurrect it — kill concepts when they stop generating money.

Tags: multi, creative-strategy, operations, content-strategy, teamwork
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Treat idea reuse as normal, but draw the line at verbatim copying
Use when: Deciding how closely a store can adapt a competitor's or creator's format without brand risk.
- Assume any idea you saw is likely a copy of a copy — the source describes content being taken from copies three degrees removed.
- Draw the practical line: no word-for-word scripts, no direct asset lifting; adaptations of an idea are, per the source, effectively 'up for grabs'.
- Accept that there is no reliable recourse even when your own content is reused; plan for the copy to happen and compete on being first and continuing to release new work.
- Especially for personal brands, being first matters more than guarding the format; the source says copiers get a fraction of the brand-deal value.
- For brands, prioritize consistency and execution over policing originality.
Caveat: This is the source's opinion ('anything goes... as long as it's not egregious'), not legal advice.
Caveat: Copyright, trademark and platform rules still apply; consult counsel for commercial use.

Tags: multi, creative-strategy, content-strategy, positioning
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Watching Brand Pages Built on Narrative, Not Product Shots
Use when: You are planning your store's social content calendar or auditing your brand's organic presence and want concrete models to imitate at your size.
- Recognize the source's pattern: Bad Ombres (a small burrito brand) tells the founder story and business-growth narrative in every format — video, carousel, stories — so followers feel they belong to a journey, not a sales feed. Adapt this by filming the people, decisions and milestones behind your product rather than only the product.
- Fotic (perfume): the founder is personally active, explaining his preferences ('I don't buy this type of bottle'), his favorite fragrances and how new releases are developed — building the store around one credible personality. If you are a founder-led store, let your actual opinions and process carry the feed.
- Belmont (hospitality): embraces carousel trends and clean visual vignettes with no text overlays; the source calls hospitality notoriously bad at social, so this is a template for experience-driven brands in underserved categories. For your store, shoot atmosphere and experience clips that need no caption to land.
- She Glam (Shein's makeup brand) and Gisou show high production value, careful audio/sound editing, fast-moving event recaps and big celebrity/food collabs built to travel on the internet. Note these are large-budget examples; the transferable piece is polish and speed, not the spend.
- Sunny's (Philippines cosmetics) shows that mid-tier, elevated-looking brand content is achievable without a giant team. Pick the one or two models closest to your budget and imitate structure, not budget.
- Treat all of these as the presenter's observations of brands, not verified performance data; test the style against your own audience before committing budget.
Caveat: These are one practitioner's named examples; he gives no metrics, so treat them as stylistic references, not proven outperformance.
Caveat: The luxury and large-brand examples (Gisou, She Glam) require resources a small store may not have.

Tags: multi, social-content, brand-narrative, content-strategy, organic-social, creative-strategy, founder-led
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Bet on Creators Early Instead of Buying Established Reach
Use when: You are selecting influencer or affiliate partners for acquisition and deciding whether to pay up for proven reach or invest early in rising creators.
- Assign this spotting job to someone on the marketing team who is 'chronically online' — the source says a person with a good gut inside their niche can call a small account's trajectory (he cites spotting a creator under 20k followers he believed had high mathematical odds of reaching 100k).
- Give the creator a simple structure or ask their dream scenario: 'when you get to 100k, what would the sponsor that helped you get there get?' — this frames an early deal both sides can grow into.
- Run this like TV upfronts: pitch content plans to partners far in advance ('I'm going to Japan and X, we're going to do this content — interested?') and ask your best existing creators what's coming next so you can get involved early.
- Honor the relationship's early days: the presenter says one of his YouTube sponsors has been with him since day one and he has never asked them to raise their rate — early support can buy loyalty and below-market rates later.
- Big luxury brands are described as doing the same talent bet (Chanel, Louis Vuitton bringing on new-wave actors alongside established stars); the principle scales down to indie stores.
- Judge on upside, not current reach: the source frames getting in ahead of performance as 'the win'.
Caveat: Spotting a rising creator is a judgment call, not a formula; the source describes gut instinct, not a scoring model.
Caveat: Early-sponsor loyalty benefits are the presenter's personal anecdote, not a guaranteed outcome.

Tags: multi, influencer-marketing, creator-partnerships, acquisition, affiliate-marketing, talent-scouting
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Run Large Campaigns as Funnel-Tied, Multi-Channel Systems
Use when: You are planning a major product launch or brand campaign across paid social, influencer and offline channels and need a sequence and stage-gate logic.
- Start with one big insight or cultural tension big enough to anchor the whole campaign. The cited example is Clue/Claude-style campaigns built on a consumer fear (e.g., losing creativity to AI) — find an equivalent fear, desire or cultural moment your brand can own.
- Map the asset sequence: an optimized hero video, photo shoots, a teaser before the launch, the campaign unveil, and promotion of the campaign after it drops.
- Recruit anchor influencers who actually appear inside the ad content and tell the backstory, then a second wave of creators who multiply the campaign once live.
- Define what success looks like and the specific metrics that unlock the next stage. The source describes scaling toward thousands of influencers per brief if metrics hit, and not doing it if they don't — set explicit go/no-go thresholds rather than deciding after spend.
- Extend outward: TV spot, international variations, and platform-by-platform checks (does it work on TikTok, streaming, etc.).
- Treat it as 1+1=3: influencer resonance, streaming ads and retail aisle-interrupters reinforcing one campaign message; the source cites Carl Jr./Alex Earl as a multi-prong moment where much of the amplification was unpaid.
- Note the presenter's critique: large brands (salesforce cited) run huge awareness ads but sometimes lose the traditional funnel basics — if the campaign had a clear ebook/course/landing-page CTA and email value per lead, it could capture demand while gaining awareness. Attach your awareness push to a measurable capture path.
Caveat: This is the presenter's campaign framework, illustrated with named examples; he provides no measured results.
Caveat: Some channels (Super Bowl, mass TV) are only available to very large budgets; the sequence logic still applies at smaller scale but the specific tactics do not.

Tags: multi, campaign-planning, launch-strategy, influencer-marketing, brand-awareness, measurement, funnel
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Manufacture Scale With Affiliates and Creative Volume, Even on a Small Team
Use when: You are resourcing your store's creative and affiliate program and deciding how many assets, angles and partners to run per month.
- Study brands scaling on TikTok Shop: the source says they will have 3,000–5,000 affiliates a month, communicate with them, and run multiple channels — while the team behind it is, in his observation, often about three people. Use this as evidence the operations ceiling is higher than most assume.
- Increase volume across everything: number of accounts, number of angles, number of pieces of creative, how many ads enter the ad account, how many influencers and creators. Lean into scale as the strategy rather than optimizing a tiny set of assets.
- Do this only after quality: the presenter explicitly says it is a waste to think about scale before you are good, and that if your one creative isn't even good, adding 5x creates nothing.
- For teams already making good work, he estimates you could probably 5x your velocity if velocity became the priority — treat that as his opinion, not a benchmark, and test whether added volume actually performs before treating it as a rule.
- Pair volume with briefs and communication workflows rather than bespoke handling of each partner, since the cited scaling brands manage thousands of affiliates at once.
Caveat: Creative volume numbers (3,000–5,000 affiliates, 3-person teams, 5x velocity) are the presenter's observations and estimates, not audited figures or promises.
Caveat: Scale without prior creative quality is explicitly called a waste by the source.

Tags: multi, creative-volume, affiliate-marketing, tiktok-shop, scaling, team-structure, content-operations
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## What Content Marketing Over- and Under-Emphasizes
Use when: You are setting creative guidelines or reviewing brand standards for ads and organic content and deciding what constraints to loosen.
- Loosen the 'always stay on brand' and 'product must be front and center' rules. The source's position: this is a storytelling world, it needs to be fluid, and if you live by old standards you will lose to a team with bias for action that isn't bound by the same requirements.
- Reset your standards around story and speed. When facing a competitor willing to ship imperfect work fast, rigid brand policing slows you down; decide which standards are load-bearing (legal, positioning) and which are inherited habit.
- Then push scale on the levers he says are underused: how many accounts you run, how many angles you test, how many pieces of creative go into the ad account, and how many influencers/creators you work with.
- Operate your store's program with more breadth than feels normal for your team size, using workflows and briefs rather than bespoke handling per asset.
- Bias for action, not standards: the source frames teams willing to act without waiting on brand sign-off as the ones that win.
Caveat: This is a strong opinion from the presenter; some categories (regulated products, luxury, healthcare) may make loosening brand control risky.
Caveat: No metrics are given to quantify the cost of over-branding; treat as directional.

Tags: multi, content-strategy, brand-guidelines, creative-strategy, bias-for-action, social-content
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

---

## Build Repeatable Infrastructure for Viral Moments Instead of One-Off Deals
Use when: Your product or brand appears in a viral social moment (a customer's post blows up) and you are deciding whether and how to respond.
- Ask the mass-market question first. The source's test: does this only appeal to a certain level of internet culture, i.e., does it go far enough? At a very large brand level, near-every-person reach is the bar, and a niche resonance may not be worth the time or the review overhead.
- Note the cited Stanley case — a woman's house burned down and her Stanley cup survived, the CEO responded, and the brand rode it. This is the practitioner's reference for a viral moment handled well.
- Distinguish the influencer from the moment. A one-off payment to a viral influencer may be a bad idea if association is off (the source raises the Shelby Sapp/Mercedes case as a possibly negative association), while the same virality via a different, on-brand person could be worth building around.
- Build an infrastructure, not a single response: the source describes a Mercedes-style framework where any viral Mercedes moment has a defined pipeline — send a custom package, launch an ad campaign, pay X, have the team show up — run a hundred times. Design your own version so activation doesn't require a from-scratch decision each time.
- Gate on execution capability: even with unlimited budget there's no unlimited time. If a launch produces 900 views or looks sponsored, it damages the brand, so only activate when your team can credibly make the resulting content hit.
Caveat: The Stanley and Mercedes examples are the presenter's illustrations, not verified campaign results.
Caveat: Whether a viral moment 'goes far enough' is a judgment call; the source gives no measurement method.

Tags: multi, viral-marketing, brand-safety, influencer-marketing, campaign-planning, infrastructure
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Don't Over-Rely on One Big Celebrity Placement
Use when: You are weighing a large single influencer or celebrity buy against spreading budget across many creators and formats.
- Separate two uses of a huge creator: (1) treating them as a celebrity guest in your ad (the source calls this 'oddball' — he says he would not pay MrBeast $5M just to appear in a Shopify ad), versus (2) having them make the most viral piece of content that contains your brand. Choose the second framing.
- Scale the second way if you're big: for an Adobe-size brand, the cited right move is 'get everybody' — sponsor as many creators as you can, enable them to make good creative, and tie it to one overarching campaign idea.
- Tie every large creator spend back to funnel stages. The source complains that big brands lose the traditional basics (landing page, download, email metrics, email campaign over time) in pursuit of high-scale promotion — decide your LP, offer and email capture before the spend runs.
- For paying attention as a strategy, budget for scale plus a clear metric: think of it as 'cheap eyeballs vs expensive eyeballs' economics; the gambling-ad example is just buying cheap eyeballs, which is a legitimate strategy only if you actually have the budget to think that way.
- Align paid and organic: Clue-style paid support runs behind the influencer niche they found, rather than replacing it.
Caveat: The MrBeast and Adobe examples are opinions in the source, with no campaign performance data.
Caveat: The 'get everybody' model requires budgets and team throughput most independent stores lack.

Tags: multi, influencer-marketing, celebrity-partnerships, budgeting, funnel, paid-media
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Scale Creators Into a Niche Your Competitors Ignore (Clue Model)
Use when: You are deciding where to focus acquisition spend and creator partnerships to find reach competitors don't own.
- Start small: the source did one of Clue's first influencer efforts, then they noticed it worked and scaled hard into a targeted angle — female creative content makers with a more intellectual, thoughtful style.
- Read the signal: 10 or 11 creators producing good results became a signal that this audience converts and that they were reaching people competitors weren't.
- Dominate the niche instead of diversifying: they sponsored essentially all of them and now run hundreds of creators in that campaign, then ran paid media behind it. The lesson is 'hammer one initiative,' not run 100 separate ones.
- Use size as a moat: 'what new things are we doing (streaming, influence) that we can scale at a level others can't?' is the framing he says to think with at large budgets.
- Pair it with monoculture moments (Super Bowl, Olympics, Black Friday, Valentine's Day) — the source says those remaining shared moments are undervalued, referencing Clue's mass-TV launch and a follow-up Super Bowl concept.
- For a small store, adapt by dominating a specific creator niche you can afford to saturate rather than a single large buy.
Caveat: Clue's results are cited as an example, not measured proof; the presenter describes the strategy, not data tables.
Caveat: Saturating any niche with hundreds of creators requires budget and deal-making capacity.

Tags: multi, influencer-marketing, acquisition, audience-segmentation, paid-media, scaling
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Judge Ad Buys by Audience and Deal Size, Not Raw Listeners
Use when: You are buying podcast, newsletter or creator sponsorships and need a way to decide if the price is justified.
- Reject the raw audience-count comparison. The source references TBPN (a podcast) where critics say ad spots cost ~$1M and only reach ~5,000 listeners — he argues that misses the point: ask who the people are, what decision level they sit at, and what the average deal size is.
- For high-AOV software/SaaS-style buyers, the economics differ sharply: if first-year AOV is $10k, cost per lead can be far higher and still work. Apply this when you're selling expensive or high-LTV products and picking sponsorship targets.
- Ask the audience question directly: does this show/platform speak to the audience you need, and can you articulate that clearly? The source says TBPN articulates it through the talent interacting with it, and that X (Twitter) makes this easier to see than other networks.
- Use CPM as one input, not the decision, when your objective is leads and revenue per customer rather than reach.
Caveat: The $1M/5,000-listeners and $10k AOV numbers are the presenter's illustrations, not benchmarks.
Caveat: This reasoning applies best to high-AOV or high-LTV offers; low-ticket stores need different sponsorship math.

Tags: multi, podcast-advertising, media-buying, aov, lead-generation, measurement
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Spot and Hire the Creative Strategist Role (15-20k+ Range Cited)
Use when: You are hiring a marketing lead, content director or creative strategist for your store and need to define the role and screening criteria.
- Define the role as tactical and cross-functional, not a glorified project manager. The source says the director of marketing is now either a head of content/social or more like a creative director who influences how good everything is across ads and organic — the project-manager version 'can't exist in this new world.'
- When a new initiative (e.g., conquering a new channel) exceeds that person's bandwidth or expertise, hire a specialist for that specific channel rather than expecting one generalist to be a unicorn.
- Screen for the trait he says is consistent among the killers: creative people who found a way to organize. When you find someone who keeps a reporting framework, a few spreadsheets, and a list of every influencer they've ever worked with — and has any degree of creativity — put them in the role.
- Handle the gap between tactician and strategist: creative skill set first, then bolt on strategy, network and experience, which is how one becomes a creative director.
- Budget: all offers he is seeing start at $120k low, $150k+ typical — treat as a source-reported range, and note the role is in demand from info-product people and creators who need influence support.
- Attract them by offering creatively interesting projects with interesting people that can blow up, with few constraints — the source says every creative wants that environment and leaves as soon as it isn't true.
- Add skin in the game: he cites spiffing an organic strategist for organic posts that also scale on paid, giving a big incentive while they learned paid, because the role is worth a lot if it actually generates revenue.
- Consider a training path if you can't hire the finished profile: assignments, feedback and ongoing work on the missing skill (e.g., email marketing) are described as how this gap is being filled. Note the source has a product selling into that gap, so treat this as his commercial perspective.
Caveat: Salary figures ($120k low, $150k+ typical) are the presenter's observed range, not a market survey.
Caveat: The training-gap solution is described by someone actively selling into that gap.

Tags: multi, hiring, marketing-team, creative-strategist, role-design, compensation, talent
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Choose Between a Flat Store Team and an Agency by Fit, Not Ambition
Use when: You are deciding whether to build in-house marketing capacity, hire a freelancer, or work with an agency for your store.
- Run the competitor test the source implies: the strategist role requires giving feedback to media buyers where you can tell them a creative is right or wrong with conviction. He says it's hard, and people who know they'd fail at giving that feedback won't sign up — assess whether you or your hire can actually perform it.
- Recognize where conviction comes from: the presenter says his conviction in judging hooks came only from making content himself; if you need that judgment in-house, build it by producing, not just reviewing.
- Apply this to ecommerce decisions directly: if nobody on your team can confidently call a bad hook or a weak angle, you'll either rely on an agency for that judgment or invest in someone who has earned it.
- State the honest limitation: the source does not present a rule for choosing agency vs. in-house, only the observation that the strategy work is hard enough that unequipped people won't attempt it — so make the choice based on demonstrated capability and give feedback on actual work.
Caveat: This is the presenter's observation about who attempts the role, not a tested decision framework.
Caveat: No criteria or thresholds are given for agency-vs-in-house selection.

Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Treat Creative People as Underpriced and Remove the Monetization Stigma
Use when: You are structuring creative roles, pay and incentives in your store's marketing function, or you are a creative deciding whether to monetize your skills.
- Name the belief barrier: the source says creatives have been taught that monetizing art means selling out, that insecurity is rampant among them, and that agencies historically kept junior copywriters/art directors at ~$68k and laid them off first — which he says is obsolete. As a store owner, this means you may be able to hire excellent creative talent at below its current market value.
- Use proof to build conviction: he says his own certainty in judging hooks came from making content, and once you have that certainty about one network, cracking a second network feels achievable. Structure junior creative roles to include actual publishing so judgment compounds.
- Pay for outcomes, not titles: he says a creative who can make things move on the internet is worth significantly more than their boss, and cites spiffing an organic strategist for posts that also scaled on paid — tie creative compensation to revenue-attached outcomes.
- Watch for the failure mode: loudest is often most insecure, per the source, and these cultural issues only get solved when a creative puts work out, gets success and compares rates with peers.
- For roles with a public-facing component you may need to provide the ego support — visible work, public wins, upside — because the source says only so many people make the jump to claiming their market worth.
Caveat: The $68k junior-copywriter figure is the presenter's characterization of agency pay, not a current market rate.
Caveat: The claims about creative psychology are the presenter's observations, not research findings.

Tags: multi, creative-talent, compensation, team-building, marketing-team, content-operations
Source: Every Level of Marketing.docx

## Coordinate evidence and communications when product claims are challenged
Use when: A product claim (calorie count, ingredient, efficacy) is challenged publicly or goes viral on social media and you must decide how to respond.
- Preserve the challenged claims, supporting tests and relevant communications.
- Have appropriate technical and legal reviewers establish what is known, disputed and suitable to communicate.
- Choose response timing and channel based on customer needs and the actual dispute, not a universal rule to respond publicly.
- Explain substantiated facts plainly without asserting contested allegations as settled.
- Monitor customer questions and update the response when verified information changes.
Caveat: The source's founder response is an anecdote, not a legal playbook or a verified account of the underlying dispute.

Tags: multi, brand, viral-pr, crisis-management, regulatory-claims, social-media, food-cpg
Source: He Built a $725 Million Company in 255 Days. Here's What You're Doing Wrong.docx

## Acquire your sole-source ingredient supplier to remove scaling risk
Use when: Your product depends on a proprietary or single-source ingredient that limits how far you can scale or exposes you to price and availability risk.
- Identify the ingredient that carries your product's differentiation, such as the EPG fat replacer that lowers calories roughly 50% without a taste trade-off.
- Assess dependency: if one supplier controls the input, that supplier sits between you and growth and holds pricing leverage.
- Structure the acquisition, which Rahal did with a cash-and-equity deal, so the supplier's incentives align with your growth rather than against it.
- Also negotiate a Most Favored Nation (MFN) clause in supply agreements so you get the best pricing and inventory availability terms the supplier offers anyone.
- Treat the acquisition as both a cost-control and a moat move: you gain the formulation IP and the ability to extend it into new categories such as ice cream and fried foods.
Caveat: Buying a supplier adds operating complexity and capital risk; it is a bet that your product line scales enough to justify owning it.
Caveat: The MFN definition and enforceability depend on the contract; verify actual terms with counsel rather than assuming best-price protection.
Caveat: Rahal's EPG calorie-reduction figure is his own product claim, not an independent benchmark.

Tags: multi, supply-chain, vertical-integration, cogs, ingredient-ip, product-moat, mfn-clause
Source: He Built a $725 Million Company in 255 Days. Here's What You're Doing Wrong.docx

## Design packaging around a saturated category claim
Use when: Your product packaging or PDP hero image competes in a category where every label makes the same claim (protein, low-calorie, natural).
- Name the saturated claim (Rahal cites 'protein' as the saturated word) and deliberately avoid competing on it visually.
- Use negative space and simplicity. RXBAR led with the ingredient list, 'three egg whites, two dates...' instead of the logo, so the ingredient story itself became the design.
- Reduce the logo's prominence so the product's substance leads; the packaging becomes a transparency statement.
- Bring in deliberate tension where it fits the brand: David Protein used gold and feminine design cues against a masculine name to create memorable contrast.
- Consider inverting hierarchy: decide whether brand or flavor is the primary identifier and flip the conventional order if the category is uniform.
- Test the shelf or thumbnail at small size to confirm the ingredient-led design still communicates.
Caveat: Contrarian design is a positioning bet, not a guaranteed conversion lift; it depends on the category being truly saturated.
Caveat: Ingredient-led design requires the ingredient story to be genuinely distinctive; a weak formula exposes itself.
Caveat: These are the founder's design choices and reasoning, not tested conversion benchmarks.

Tags: multi, brand, packaging, product-page, creative-strategy, differentiation, merchandising
Source: He Built a $725 Million Company in 255 Days. Here's What You're Doing Wrong.docx

## Apply the 'non-obvious but true' test to marketing ideas
Use when: You are choosing campaign angles, ad hooks, content concepts or brand stunts and need a filter beyond 'does it get attention.'
- Generate the obvious version first so you can see it. Rahal labels 'David vs Goliath' as obvious, meaning overused and forgettable.
- Look for the non-obvious but true alternative. Comparing a protein bar to boiled cod is his example of surprising yet logically defensible.
- Check that the surprising claim is true; the framework only works when the audience can accept the premise after the surprise.
- Apply it to stunts and PR as well as ads: the same filter governs the lawsuit response and the truck wraps in New York.
- Pair non-obvious creative with credible distribution, such as podcaster sponsorships with hosts like Huberman and Lane Norton, where the audience already trusts the host's judgment.
- Keep a running list of obvious/overused angles in your category so you can consciously reject them.
Caveat: 'Non-obvious but true' is a creative heuristic, not a measurable performance rule; it can still produce campaigns that fail.
Caveat: A surprising claim that is not defensibly true becomes a credibility or legal problem.

Tags: multi, brand, creative-strategy, acquisition, campaign-planning, positioning
Source: He Built a $725 Million Company in 255 Days. Here's What You're Doing Wrong.docx

## Stage a pre-launch with anticipation, free drops and an owned list
Use when: You are preparing a new product or brand launch and want demand in place on day one.
- Build anticipation over months by posting the build process on LinkedIn and X, which Rahal did for roughly six months before David Protein launched.
- Give product away at volume rather than hoarding it. David gave away 5,000 bars on TikTok to create first-hand experience and user content.
- Accumulate an owned audience in parallel; the company had a 40,000-person email list ready at launch.
- Coordinate channels so the giveaway and the social documentation feed the same audience that the launch email reaches.
- Reinvest early attention into retail conversations; pre-launch proof of demand is what regional grocery buyers respond to.
- Track list growth and engagement as leading indicators rather than waiting for launch-week sales.
Caveat: Free-product giveaways are a real cost and a bet; Rahal's 5,000-bar drop is a chosen spend, not a proven formula.
Caveat: A 40,000-person launch list is a specific outcome of this company, not a benchmark to target.
Caveat: Viral social attention is unpredictable and cannot be guaranteed by following the playbook.

## Position a sensitive category without triggering the category's stigma
Use when: Your product sits in a stigmatized or tired category (weight loss, diet, budget) and you need positioning and audience definition that sidesteps the stigma.
- Name the stigma explicitly. Rahal wanted a weight-loss company that did not carry the baggage of brands like Jenny Craig.
- Define the ICP around identity rather than a clinical need: optimizers, biohackers, models and GLP-1 users who already track protein and calories.
- Map the product to a macro-trend with a concrete job to be done, such as GLP-1 induced muscle loss, rather than a vague 'healthy living' claim.
- Let audience language drive the message; newly differentiated groups respond to specificity about their goals, not generic wellness promises.
- Keep the product's promise (high protein, low calorie) aligned with what these users already measure and optimize.
- Sequence the niche-to-mass expansion deliberately; Rahal's RXBAR grew from CrossFit niches toward mainstream distribution.
Caveat: Rahal's GLP-1 and ICP framing is his own market read, not a validated segmentation study.
Caveat: Niche-first positioning can ceiling your early volume; expansion requires revisiting the message.
Caveat: Stigmatized-category products may still face regulatory scrutiny over health-related claims.

Tags: multi, positioning, customer-research, icp, product-research, glp1, brand
Source: He Built a $725 Million Company in 255 Days. Here's What You're Doing Wrong.docx

## Sequence retail expansion from regional to mass
Use when: You are planning retail distribution for a new or premium CPG product and choosing which accounts to pursue first.
- Start with regional grocery such as Wegmans or Publix, where buyers can back an unproven premium brand and store-level attention is possible.
- Delay mass-market national retail until you have proof of sell-through in those accounts; RXBAR failed at Walmart initially because it read as too premium for that shopper.
- Use regional wins as social proof and velocity data when approaching larger accounts.
- Adjust price, pack or message for value-oriented retailers before pitching them, rather than presenting the premium version.
- Treat retail as a sequence of small bites; each account converts to data and credibility for the next.
Caveat: Rahal's RXBAR example is a specific historical outcome, not a rule that Walmart always rejects premium products.
Caveat: Retail sequencing depends on category, price point and retailer buyer behavior; verify current retail requirements before planning.
Caveat: Regional-first slows early revenue compared with a lucky national launch.

Tags: multi, retail, distribution, go-to-market, pricing, channel-strategy
Source: He Built a $725 Million Company in 255 Days. Here's What You're Doing Wrong.docx

## Calculate DTC gross margin including every fulfillment cost
Use when: You are pricing a DTC product or deciding whether a unit economics model supports selling direct.
- Build the margin from the product's true landed COGS, not just ingredient and packaging cost.
- Subtract final-mile shipping, 3PL pick-and-pack, and payment transaction fees before calling the result gross margin.
- Account for marketplace fees, including Amazon, if that channel is part of the plan.
- Target the 40-50% DTC gross margin range Rahal cites as the level at which CPG math works from the start.
- Hold this standard at launch rather than projecting margin improvement later; the model should be viable immediately.
- Recheck margin whenever shipping rates, packaging or channel mix change.
Caveat: The 40-50% figure is Rahal's stated heuristic for CPG DTC, not a uniform benchmark; categories and price points differ.
Caveat: Underestimating fulfillment costs is the common failure mode he warns about.
Caveat: Margin targets interact with customer acquisition cost and repeat rate, which are not covered by this margin rule alone.

Tags: multi, unit-economics, fin, dtc, gross-margin, fulfillment, pricing
Source: He Built a $725 Million Company in 255 Days. Here's What You're Doing Wrong.docx
