## Shift from ROAS to financial-based KPIs for scaling decisions
Use when: You are setting the north-star metric for your store's paid media and deciding what to optimize.
- Identify the trap: optimizing to numbers that do not match what is actually occurring in the business, often ROAS inflated by view-throughs, brand, and bottom-funnel capture.
- Understand the consequences chain: a measurement problem drives bad decision-making loops, and brands attribute credit to the wrong funnel stage.
- Move toward financial-based KPIs (e.g., new-customer profit contribution, blended CAC, incremental return) rather than platform-reported ROAS as the north star.
- Add incrementality tests at larger revenue levels to validate those financial KPIs.
- At any level, prioritize cleaning up in-platform reporting as the first step.
- Ecommerce application: for a store deciding where to scale, base the call on new-customer profit and CAC rather than a reported ROAS that may overattribute.
Caveat: This is the source's strategic opinion, framed as where winning brands are headed in 2026-2027; the source also has a commercial interest in providing audits.

Tags: multi, measurement, attribution, kpi, cac, incrementality, strategy
Source: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

---

## Calculate CAC and LTGP monthly as your two core operating metrics
Use when: You need a single monthly scorecard to decide whether the store can profitably scale paid acquisition, cut spend, or fix retention.
- Compute CAC = total ad spend across all platforms in the period divided by new customers acquired in that same period. Pull new customers from your own order data, not from a platform summary.
- Compute LTGP = gross profit from a customer over a fixed window, where gross profit means revenue minus cost of goods AND cost of delivery (shipping/fulfilment), not just revenue minus COGS.
- Choose the window based on how often your category repeats: use first-purchase gross profit (a very short window) for repurchase-poor categories like furniture and homewares; extend to roughly 180 or 365 days for consumables, supplements and subscription models.
- Pull the lifetime figure from a real cohort analysis (cohorts of customers by acquisition month, tracked forward to day 30/60/90/etc.), not from attributed revenue dashboards, daily returning-customer revenue, or a 'percent new customers' Shopify tile.
- Record both numbers every month in one table so you can see the trend. When either CAC rises or LTGP falls, drill into that metric first rather than assuming it is a creative, seasonality or traffic problem.
- Timestamp every structural change (new product, new channel, new agency, heavier discounting) and read it against the CAC and LTGP series to see whether the change improved the ratio, then double down or reverse.
Caveat: Applying an assumed gross-margin percentage to cohort revenue is a workaround; the source says generating it from actual cost of goods is better.
Caveat: Platform-attributed ROAS can stay stable while the real business declines, because view-through and over-crediting inflate it.

Tags: measurement, profit-and-contribution, customer-acquisition-cost, cohort-analysis, ltgp-cac, unit-economics
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Read the LTGP:CAC bands and know what each one demands
Use when: You are setting a paid-media budget or deciding whether to push spend harder, hold, or pull back on acquisition.
- Diagnose your current position: if LTGP is $100 and CAC is $120, the ratio is below 1 and you lose $20 on the first purchase. The source treats sub-1 as structurally dangerous unless retention is genuinely exceptional, which it calls very rare.
- Recognise the 1-2 band as workable but tight: at $1 in and $1.50 out in gross profit, the 50 cents must cover operating expenses, so you need unusually lean opex or very large volume to produce a healthy net margin. The source says it is possible to run here with strong operations and retention, just uncommon.
- Treat 2-3 as the zone where the source always suggests scaling and ramping budgets.
- Treat above 3 as a signal you are leaving money on the table and should ramp harder.
- Do not chase a fantasy ratio: LTGP is bounded by category structure. A low-ticket product (e.g. a $50 supplement) cannot deliver an arbitrary multiple, so benchmark against the best operators in your own category and set a realistic CAC target from there.
Caveat: These bands are the presenter's heuristics for DTC ecommerce, not a universal law, and they assume ecommerce dynamics (weak consumer stickiness) rather than service or B2B models.
Caveat: The bands assume LTGP is measured over the correct window for your repurchase frequency; comparing a 30-day LTGP to a 365-day CAC benchmark is meaningless.

Tags: measurement, ltgp-cac, unit-economics, media-buying, scaling, profit-and-contribution
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Derive CAC from CPM, CTR and conversion rate to offset rising ad costs
Use when: Your CAC is climbing and you need to decide which lever — ad creative, PDP/landing page conversion, or media efficiency — to work on.
- Write out the chain: CAC = CPC / conversion rate and CPC = CTR x CPM, so CPM sits several layers beneath CAC via CPC.
- Accept the structural premise the source states: platforms need to grow revenue every year, so CPMs will very likely be higher next year. Plan for it rather than treating it as a crisis.
- Offset that lift by improving either CTR or conversion rate. If you lift one of them enough, you hold your profitability roughly flat year over year even as CPMs rise.
- For ecommerce application: CTR improvements come from creative and offer framing in the ad, while conversion-rate improvements come from the PDP, landing page, offer clarity, pricing presentation and checkout. Assign the fix to the right surface rather than defaulting to 'creative'.
- Set a discipline of compounding small improvements — the source frames it as improving about 1% a day on CTR and conversion. Operators who stay better than the majority keep feeling less CPM pressure and can push budget harder when competitors pull back.
- Note that platform algorithm updates are designed to lift advertiser ROI so the platform can then raise CPMs; the platform does not hand you the surplus, so your own improvement is the offset.
Caveat: This is a decomposition, not a prediction; conversion rate here means purchase conversion on your traffic, not lead conversion.
Caveat: CTR and CPM interact with audience and placement; a CTR gain on cheap placements may not translate into cheaper CAC.

Tags: measurement, customer-acquisition-cost, conversion-optimization, creative-strategy, paid-social, media-buying
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Split the P&L into first-time and returning customer views
Use when: Total profit still looks acceptable but you suspect new-customer acquisition has quietly turned loss-making, or before raising capital or debt.
- Tag orders in your commerce platform by first-time versus returning customer, then generate two full P&Ls by filtering every line item on that tag.
- Read total profit contribution at the bottom of each. A brand can lose, illustratively, $50,000 a month on the first-time-customer P&L while making $300,000 on the returning-customer P&L, so the business looks profitable while acquisition is bleeding.
- Track the trend in the first-time P&L specifically: the source's example is a client falling from +$20,000/month on first-time customers to -$70,000/month, invisible in the blended view.
- Use this split when deciding whether returning revenue is genuinely subsidising acquisition or merely masking it. If returning profit is not covering the first-time loss, the model is fragile and any retention wobble becomes an existential event.
- If a full split is impractical, use the unit-level LTGP:CAC ratio as the everyday proxy — the source says it tells you the same story at unit level that the P&L split tells you at volume level.
- Pair the split with a cohort view of CAC month over month and new-customer volume month over month, since the pattern the source describes is CAC exploding and spend being cranked up to hold volume, after which CAC never recovers.
Caveat: Requires reliable order-type tagging; mis-tagged orders corrupt both P&Ls.
Caveat: The dollar figures cited are illustrative case examples from the presenter's audits, not benchmarks for your store.

Tags: measurement, profit-and-contribution, customer-acquisition-cost, ltgp-cac, retention, financial-modeling
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Diagnose the death spiral from the two numbers, not from traffic, creative or seasonality
Use when: Revenue or profitability has deteriorated for a quarter and leadership is blaming traffic, creative fatigue, seasonality or the macroeconomy.
- Trace the described loop: CAC creeps from, say, $50 to $60; at a fixed $100,000 budget you acquire fewer customers; revenue falls; with weak repeat purchasing you increase spend to hold revenue; the extra spend pushes CAC higher again, and it can end up double the prior level.
- Before accepting any other explanation, pull CAC month over month alongside new-customer volume and revenue month over month. The signature is CAC breaking upward and spend being cranked up afterwards to maintain volume.
- Reject the three default misdiagnoses the source names — that it is a traffic problem (just needs more spend or cheaper CPCs), a creative problem (creative drives targeting so it must be the ads), or a seasonality/macro problem. In the source's experience across 1,000+ audits, it is usually none of these.
- Work backwards from LTGP and CAC to identify the actual constraint, then fix that constraint rather than adding spend on top of a broken unit economic.
- Be aware that forcing scale through a bad LTGP with raised capital does not work; the source states that the ratio, not the funding, determines whether the business can scale.
Caveat: The source acknowledges operating expenses can also sink brands, particularly smaller ones ($50k-$300k/month), often causing cash-constrained failure rather than a pure LTGP:CAC failure.
Caveat: The audit volume and client scale cited are the presenter's own experience, not an independent study.

Tags: measurement, ltgp-cac, customer-acquisition-cost, media-buying, scaling, diagnostics
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Rank your measurement methods by distance from base reality
Use when: You need to decide how much to trust a platform-reported number before reallocating budget between channels or scaling spend.
- Place methods on the ladder: expert opinion plus anecdote at the bottom, then simple correlation (platform-attributed ROAS), then advanced correlation such as multi-regression or marketing mix modelling, then quasi-experiments such as difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity, then true experiments such as geo holdouts at the top.
- Prefer the highest rung you can practically run for the decision at hand; the source's framing is that the highest-ROI activity in business is making the correct decision, which requires seeing reality as clearly as possible.
- Sanity-check platform numbers by removing view-through conversions first. In the source's example, a reported ROAS that looked like ~20 collapsed to ~7 once view-throughs were stripped out, and dropped again when narrowed to a stricter attribution model.
- Watch the de-inflated number over time rather than the topline: a de-inflated figure declining month over month is the early warning the topline hides.
- Where you spend across multiple platforms, use experimental design (holdouts, quasi-experiments) to attribute contribution, because LTGP:CAC alone cannot tell you which platform drove the good or bad result.
- Keep LTGP:CAC as the ultimate scorecard of business health even while using experiments to explain why it moved.
Caveat: The source explicitly says avoiding all of this by simply watching LTGP:CAC is acceptable for many operators — the hierarchy is for platform-level attribution decisions.
Caveat: The specific ROAS collapse figures are a single anonymised client example.

Tags: measurement, incrementality-and-holdouts, attribution, experiment-design, media-buying, marketing-mix
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Match your CAC discipline to the retention structure of your category
Use when: You are setting the measurement window and CAC target for your category, or deciding whether to invest in retention or defend acquisition cost.
- Classify your category's repeat behaviour. The source cites day-365 gross-profit lift benchmarks of about 55% for fashion, about 110% for CPG and supplements, and near 0% for furniture and homewares.
- For repurchase-poor categories (furniture, homewares), treat lifetime gross profit as effectively nonexistent and manage the business on first-purchase gross profit with a stable CAC. The source's operational guidance for these clients is to keep CAC flat over time.
- For categories with genuine repeat behaviour (fashion, CPG, supplements, subscription), extend the LTGP window out to around 180-365 days and use cohort data to measure it, while still keeping CAC controlled.
- Do not assume retention tactics can transform a low-lift category. The source argues the achievable LTGP band is largely structurally predetermined by industry and price point, and that executing many retention tactics will not move a number that the business model fixes.
- Pick CAC benchmarks from the best operators in your specific industry rather than from cross-industry ratios, then aim to approach them.
- Recognise the source's own estimate that roughly 80% of brands have weak lifetime gross profit contribution (often only 20-40% gross-profit lift by day 365), in which case CAC control is the primary lever.
Caveat: The 55% / 110% / near-0% figures are the presenter's cited vertical benchmarks, not a universal measurement standard.
Caveat: B2B has materially different repeat dynamics from D2C and is called out as a different game.

Tags: measurement, retention, ltgp-cac, customer-acquisition-cost, category-strategy, cohort-analysis
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Use cohort analysis to read retention instead of surface retention metrics
Use when: You want to measure retention properly to set your LTGP window and confirm whether recent acquisition cohorts are degrading.
- Open cohort analysis and read month zero as revenue from a customer on day one, then follow the same cohort forward to day 30, 60, 90 and beyond to see its cumulative value.
- Reject the metrics the source explicitly disqualifies for this purpose: Klaviyo attributed revenue, returning-customer revenue measured daily or monthly, and the percentage-of-new-customers tile in Shopify.
- Pull the column matching your chosen window (for example the day-90 column) and convert that revenue to gross profit using actual cost of goods where possible.
- Compare that LTGP figure to the CAC recorded in the acquisition month for the same cohort to produce a windowed LTGP:CAC ratio per cohort.
- Look across cohorts, not just in aggregate: the source's example is November cohorts being markedly worse than adjacent months because of product portfolio changes and margin compression from discounting, which drags the extended lifetime window down.
- Use the cohort view to spot margin compression: even when CAC is stable month to month, first-purchase gross profit can swing from, illustratively, $70 to $40 depending on discounting and portfolio mix.
Caveat: Native cohort reporting may not display gross profit, so the source builds a custom cohort analysis to get GP rather than revenue.
Caveat: The illustrative $70/$40 and November-cohort examples are from anonymised client audits, not general benchmarks.

Tags: measurement, cohort-analysis, retention, profit-and-contribution, unit-economics, shopify
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Three legitimate ways to fund a sub-1 LTGP:CAC — and who should not use them
Use when: You are deliberately losing money on first purchase and must choose how the gap gets financed, or you are evaluating whether to take investment or debt to scale acquisition.
- Option one: fund it with repeat purchase. If returning-customer profit contribution reliably exceeds the first-time-customer loss, the business is profitable overall even while acquisition loses money. Verify with the two-P&L split rather than assuming.
- Option two: raise capital. The source does not call this inherently bad and notes that many fast-scaling DTC brands used capital to drive content network effects and aggressive ad scaling.
- Option three: use creditors/debt. The source's caution is that debt makes profitability visibility more complex, so it requires a dialled-in operator.
- Screen yourself against the source's stated threshold: it would not work with a $6-7m revenue brand carrying investors or creditors, calling the risk profile enormous and saying it has rarely seen them do well. This is an opinion, not a rule.
- Regardless of funding source, keep measuring LTGP:CAC monthly so the funding decision is based on the real acquisition economics rather than a blended P&L that looks fine.
Caveat: The source's position on not serving $6-7m brands with investors or creditors is that presenter's own risk preference and agency policy, not a universal law.
Caveat: None of these options fixes a structurally negative ratio; they only buy time to fix it.

Tags: unit-economics, ltgp-cac, profit-and-contribution, financial-modeling, scaling, customer-acquisition-cost
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Treat operating-expense creep as a separate cash-risk failure mode from the death spiral
Use when: You are setting opex and hiring plans for a smaller store (roughly $50k-$300k/month) and must protect working capital for inventory.
- Track whether margin is being compressed by opex growth, not just by CAC or COGS. The source's diagnosis of many small brands is that they overinvested in operating expenses while being poor capital allocators.
- Model the downstream effect: compressed margin leaves less cash, which pushes you to take debt to purchase future inventory, which pressures the whole financial position and can end in failure from a cash constraint rather than a bad LTGP:CAC.
- Before adding fixed cost, confirm your current LTGP:CAC can carry it. The source notes that a better ratio would have paid for the opex in these cases, so the ratio is still the root fix.
- If your store sits in the low band of LTGP:CAC (1-2), apply extra scrutiny to every fixed-cost addition, because that band requires unusually lean operating expenses to produce acceptable net profit.
- Distinguish this failure mode explicitly from the acquisition death spiral when diagnosing a declining store, so you apply the right corrective action.
Caveat: This observation is drawn from the presenter's early-agency experience with roughly 300-400 SMB ecommerce brands over three years, not a controlled study.
Caveat: The $50k-$300k/month band is the source's observed range for this pattern, not a hard threshold.

Tags: profit-and-contribution, financial-modeling, working-capital, unit-economics, scaling, ltgp-cac
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Treat first-purchase liquidity as the ecommerce norm, not the service-business norm
Use when: You are setting payback expectations and acquisition targets, and deciding whether to accept a long first-purchase payback period.
- Stop importing service-business logic. The source notes agencies often break even around month 4-6 after acquisition costs because businesses repeat-transact for years; consumers are lucky to make a second purchase and rarer still a third.
- Set the ecommerce default to near-breakeven or better on the first purchase, and treat anything materially below that as a risk position unless retention is genuinely exceptional.
- If your LTGP:CAC is below 1, quantify the requirement precisely: applying an assumed percentage of cohort revenue to get gross profit and using an illustrative $100 LTGP against a $120 CAC gives a $20 first-purchase loss per customer.
- If you must run a long payback, make it survivable with genuine measured repeat revenue rather than hoped-for retention — see the two-P&L split for verification.
- Communicate the difference in expectation internally: this card is about purchase conversion and repeat purchasing, not sales close rate or lead conversion, which follow different payback logic.
Caveat: The source's framing assumes D2C consumer behaviour; B2B and service models have different stickiness and payback tolerance.
Caveat: The $100/$120 example is illustrative arithmetic, not an industry standard.

Tags: unit-economics, customer-acquisition-cost, ltgp-cac, profit-and-contribution, retention, measurement
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Use owned channels for returning revenue while accepting that new acquisition is rented
Use when: You are allocating effort between paid acquisition and list/community ownership, or pushback arises that paid should be abandoned in favour of owned channels.
- Classify your demand sources: renting is paying for traffic that disappears when payment stops; owning is assets you keep, such as an email list, an SMS list, or a community.
- Direct owned-channel effort primarily at the LTGP side of the equation, since the source says list and community value largely sits under returning-customer revenue and drives repeat purchase.
- Accept that new-customer acquisition remains rented in most forms. The source's reasoning: you acquire a customer first and only then hold first-party data to remarket to, and even large organic followings do not guarantee delivery of a post to that audience.
- Do not adopt the dogma that you should never pay for attention. Keep improving owned assets while continuing to rent space to bring in new customers, then convert them into owned relationships.
- Note the source's defence of the 'own your list' rhetoric as correct but incomplete — it is a large and worthwhile focus on the retention side, not a replacement for paid acquisition.
Caveat: The source is explicitly arguing against the position that rising CPMs mean paid is dead and email is the answer.
Caveat: Organic reach limitations are illustrated by the presenter's own account (roughly 50,000 followers getting far fewer views per post) — an anecdote, not a platform-wide measurement.

Tags: retention, acquisition, email-marketing, ltgp-cac, paid-social, channel-strategy
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Timestamp and measure big structural changes against CAC and LTGP
Use when: You are deciding whether to repeat, roll back or expand an investment such as a product launch, a new ad platform, or a change in creative partner.
- Before making the change, record the current CAC and LTGP baseline and the date the change goes live.
- After the change, compare the post-change values against the historical series. The source's example: a March product launch that raised LTGP — expected, because portfolio diversity increases cross-sell opportunity.
- Ask explicitly whether the ratio improved, and then whether you can afford to repeat the action without putting the balance sheet at risk.
- Double down and iterate in the direction of changes that demonstrably improved the ratio rather than judging them on gut feel or a single month's revenue.
- Apply the same test to structural decisions such as introducing a new platform (e.g. Snapchat) or significantly increasing ad volume, since those consume capital and must earn their place on the ratio.
- Avoid the failure pattern the source describes: a store whose monthly profit slid from, illustratively, $100,000 to $80,000 while nobody checked the first-time-customer P&L, which had swung from positive to deeply negative.
Caveat: Requires sufficient data after each change to separate signal from normal variance; short windows may mislead.
Caveat: The $100k/$80k and March-launch examples are from anonymised client work, not guaranteed outcomes.

Tags: measurement, experiment-design, ltgp-cac, product-portfolio, scaling, decision-making
Source: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

---

## Smoke test angle validation with static image ads
Use when: New product launch or angle selection: you have a modest test budget and need to find which value proposition makes people click before spending on video production.
- Take the same product-on-white image and keep it identical across variants.
- Create a white bar with bold text (a call-out) over the image, changing only the message: e.g. 'reduce anxiety', 'increase focus', 'stress release'.
- Run all variants in one simple campaign and read which call-out earns the most clicks/engagement.
- When one call-out clearly wins, expand that single angle into video rather than making video for all angles.
- For the video, decide whether the person on screen should be a man or a woman; consider not showing a face and instead showing only hands, arms or body type so more viewers can see themselves using the product.
- After the ad-level test, move scrutiny to the landing page; keep testing ad performance in-platform to compare image vs video and value prop vs value prop.
- Repeat the loop: image test, then video, then add creators, colours and regions to get more granular as winners emerge.
Caveat: The source presents this as his own starting method, not a validated universal rule.
Caveat: CPC/CPM baselines differ by niche (he cites $15-$30 CPM as niche-dependent); judge clicks against your own account history, not the source's numbers.

Tags: multi, creative-strategy, product-page, experiment-design, acquisition, ad-creative, paid-social
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Diagnose price before scaling spend
Use when: Early-stage acquisition: deciding whether to spend more budget or change pricing after a first test tranche.
- Check whether clicks and impressions are cost-effective against your own niche baseline (the source notes CPMs vary widely by audience; hitting middle-America moms is expensive).
- If people click the ad, click through to the PDP, reach the cart and then abandon, treat it as a price/value-exchange signal and change the price.
- If people buy with good unit economics, the price point is working; if they get far along and don't buy, split-test the price.
- Treat price and product playfulness as the first thing to figure out with a small learning budget, before blaming creative.
Caveat: The source frames this as his own sequencing; his $15-$30 CPM range is illustrative and niche-specific, not a benchmark.
Caveat: At larger spend and stronger email/retention assets, a cheap cost-per-cart may be worth keeping even when the final sale doesn't happen — a judgment the source reserves for brands that can monetise the backend.

Tags: multi, pricing, conversion-optimization, experiment-design, acquisition
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Tranches of cash: define what each test budget must uncover
Use when: Budget planning for a launch or a channel test: deciding how much to allocate and what questions the money must answer before it's gone.
- Before spending, write the question the tranche must answer: is my price right, which channel is most efficient, which product works, what messaging?
- Accept that a small budget learns the same things as a large budget but takes longer; velocity is the only difference.
- In the first quarter, set the total tranche you can afford and treat it as a bet you must make work (the source's own launch example was $75k-$100k).
- Run the front-end metrics in parallel with price: are people clicking the ad, clicking through the PDP, reaching the end, buying?
- If unit economics are good, keep going; if not, isolate whether the break is creative, traffic cost or price.
Caveat: The source's Breeze figures ($75k-$100k first quarter, doubling month over month) are his brand's example, not a promise.
Caveat: He notes brands that can't survive without first-purchase profitability face a harder road, particularly if the product isn't repeat-purchasable.

Tags: multi, budgeting, experiment-design, acquisition, measurement, cac-ltv
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## CAC targets anchored to LTV, not a universal number
Use when: Acquisition planning: deciding your target and ceiling CAC, and whether to run first-purchase-profitable or loss-leading campaigns.
- Estimate how long customers stay and how often they rebuy for your specific product class; the source's working CAC is $85-$90 with a ceiling around $120-$130 on bad months.
- State that target internally so media buying can be judged against it rather than daily ROAS.
- If your product has repeat purchase or product expansion, you can justify spending to break even or a small loss on the first order.
- If your product is a one-off (his examples: rugs, a t-shirt), plan to be first-order profitable because you won't recover the loss.
- During launch on a brand-new product, budget extra for market education — teaching the category that the product is legitimate and legal can be part of the CAC.
Caveat: His $85-$90 target and $120-$130 ceiling are his brand's figures and depend on his LTV; do not copy them as benchmarks.
Caveat: Loss-leading on first purchase requires confidence in retention and backend conversion; without that it is simply unprofitable spending.

Tags: multi, acquisition, cac-ltv, pricing, measurement, retention
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Organise the ad account by story, not by funnel stage
Use when: Account structure decisions for paid social: how to name, group and route campaigns and how much to rely on audience segmentation.
- Accept that the old three-tier funnel — prospecting for new customers, a value-prop middle, a discount-retargeting bottom — is now muddier and less segmented in practice.
- Stop forcing audience segmentation to control which ad a new customer sees; that control was needed when the platform couldn't be trusted to serve the right creative, and the source argues we are now in a 'trust the algorithm' era.
- Instead, build folders around your stories and angles: e.g. a 'feel better tomorrow' group that contains every video, image and landing page version of that story.
- Keep the story consistent from the landing page all the way through the ad assets inside each folder.
- Invest the saved effort into telling more convincing stories and building more offers, since landing pages can now be built or adapted in a day with current tools (verify current tools' interfaces).
Caveat: This is the source's read of platform direction and his own account practice, not a platform mandate; some accounts may still benefit from tighter segmentation.
Caveat: His claim that creative now outweighs audience selection rests on a platform engineering article he references, not on a controlled test.

Tags: multi, account-structure, creative-strategy, paid-social, landing-page, targeting
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Creative as the new targeting
Use when: Creative direction and casting for paid social: choosing who appears in ads and which regional variants to produce.
- Identify the market you're buying and match the people in the ad to it: the source reports ads with people who look like they've lived in Florida perform better in Florida, and New York-styled creative performs better in New York.
- Treat a creative as stackable bricks — hook, value prop, benefits, problem, solution — and rearrange them for each audience or product claim.
- Test granularity: for example, three women stating three effects within the first few seconds versus founders on camera; the source reports far longer retention when the viewer sees themselves.
- In the briefing, specify the placement, framing and length, plus examples of what is working and examples of what has failed, so creators know the boundaries without losing their own voice.
- Archive and reuse: keep an organised drive of past winning assets because long libraries are now a competitive asset for remixing into new clips.
Caveat: Regional-matching results are the source's own-reported observations, not published benchmarks.
Caveat: Continuously refreshing the library matters because asset styles age quickly.

Tags: multi, creative-strategy, acquisition, paid-social, briefing, targeting
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Design creative natively for each placement
Use when: Ad production and briefing: fixing poor performance caused by mismatched aspect ratios and unreadable captions on Reels and Stories.
- Decide the placements in advance (the source focuses on Meta) and produce assets at the correct ratios — he names 4x5 and 9x16 — rather than one square that gets reused everywhere.
- Check that captions and the focal point of the creative are visible instantly in the chosen ratio; square ads with words and dots in a story are a common, fixable mistake.
- In the creator brief, state the placement and format explicitly (e.g. 'this is for Meta Reels, we need 9x16 or 4x5'), plus framing rules such as shooting in sunlight.
- Build the fix into the workflow: return creator footage that is too close or has the product cut off on the right for reshooting rather than shipping it.
- Sort every concept into an image version and a video version for each placement — the source calls this more work but necessary at serious spend.
Caveat: The exact ratios and platform behaviours can change; verify current placement specs in the ad platform before briefing.
Caveat: The source says small brands may not be able to obsess at this level initially; it prioritises placement hygiene at higher spend.

Tags: multi, creative-strategy, briefing, paid-social, ad-creative, product-page
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Make the media buyer a P&L-aware creative strategist
Use when: Team design for paid acquisition: deciding the roles needed to run ads and what performance reporting the buyer should own.
- Restructure from separate pods (creative strategist, account manager, media buyer, junior buyer, designer) to one owner who is both media buyer and creative strategist, supported by a designer and creators.
- Put that person in direct contact with whoever owns creative strategy on Slack so iterations, hooks and asset formats move in real time.
- Give them visibility of the P&L and forecasting so their decisions account for the whole business, not just an ad-platform ROAS widget.
- Expect a media buyer who believes they control performance mainly through account settings to be replaced by one who manages creative supply.
- Consider using an outside expert for a short weekly check-in while someone internal learns the account — the source used this as a hedge and short-term training.
Caveat: The source's example is an internal hire who had never run an ad and was given four weeks to self-teach, supported by an existing creative team — not a guarantee for every brand.
Caveat: He also says a freelance media buyer at a high level now needs designers and editors around them; the lone button-pusher is the role at risk.

Tags: multi, team-design, paid-social, creative-strategy, measurement, cac-ltv
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Run a weekly creative volume target tied to spend
Use when: Creative operations and resourcing: setting a weekly production target and deciding when to hire editors or creators.
- Set a weekly target in concepts, not just assets — the source's example is 10 concepts with 2 ads each, 20 total, as a successful week.
- Track two numbers per week: how many new assets launched, and how many hit the success metric, which he defines as dollars spent on them.
- Adjust the target for season: product drops, Q3/Q4 and summer versus Q1 change the required volume and the profitability target.
- Use the target to size the team: if the target doubles in busy season, that tells you when to hire against it.
- Do not produce assets for SKUs that can't be sold — if products are backordered, funnel that time and money elsewhere.
- Keep roughly a 30-day runway of assets, planning monthly and rotating in drops, holidays and evergreen angles.
- When introducing new ads, avoid flooding the account: adding 5-15 new ads while only two or three proven ads carry spend can skew the whole account, which often forces the team to kill the new ads.
Caveat: The 10 concepts/20 ads figure is the source's own weekly benchmark for one brand; it shifts with season and product drops.
Caveat: Too much volume can destabilise a profitable account — the source explicitly names the tension between 'more assets' and 'we're unprofitable, kill everything'.

Tags: multi, creative-strategy, team-design, ad-creative, experiment-design, budgeting
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Think about the funnel in numbers: 70/30 to 90/10
Use when: Allocating budget inside a paid social account: how much to keep on convictions and how much to reserve for new tests.
- Target roughly 70% of dollars on assets you have conviction in and 30% on things you are unsure about.
- When overall company performance is bad, shift to 90/10 — the source says even 100/0 is defensible then.
- Time tests against where your sales actually come from: the source notes his product gets more energy Friday-Sunday, so spending heavily Monday-Thursday risks wasting budget that would perform better on the weekend.
- Let the ratio flex daily based on profitability and on the platform's allocation behaviour — if Meta shifts spend to a non-converting ad, turning it off can stop the account from spending, so the buyer has to push and pull budgets rather than letting the account run limp.
- Make sure you keep testing while new people are coming in, or the account eventually runs out of fresh winners.
Caveat: 70/30 and 90/10 are the source's heuristics, not calculated from a dataset or universal rule.
Caveat: The right ratio depends on how much proven creative you already have and how tolerant your unit economics are.

Tags: multi, budgeting, experiment-design, creative-strategy, paid-social, measurement
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Judge ads on multiple KPIs, not dashboard profit alone
Use when: Ad reporting and optimisation: deciding whether to switch off an ad or channel that looks unprofitable on its own dashboard.
- Use CAC as the primary success metric for a customer.
- Treat email or text capture as a legitimate secondary KPI: if an ad gets people to cart cheaply, the source keeps spending because the address is captured and the backend can convert later.
- Look at CPM as a softer third indicator, particularly on awareness-heavy placements that don't produce the highest-quality traffic but do reach people; the source says a small brand probably shouldn't let this drive decisions yet, while a larger one can.
- Blend channels into one pot: an ad source (his example: Apple Search Ads) may lose on CAC but win on email collection, and the company-level question is whether total channels hit the goal CAC.
- Coordinate spend with the rest of the business: if email flows, a product drop or a discount programme will land in the next days, pull back ad spend rather than overspending on customers who would buy anyway.
Caveat: The 20% subscriber take rate he cites is his brand's figure; relying on email capture assumes your own backend can convert those addresses.
Caveat: The 'let it run past profitability' approach is explicitly something he says works at his scale, not a rule for brands without strong retention and flows.

Tags: multi, measurement, retention, acquisition, cac-ltv, email-marketing, budgeting
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Match site experience to customer history
Use when: Site merchandising and CRM: deciding what a visitor sees on arrival based on purchase history.
- For a visitor who has never bought, communicate the SKUs they should try first, chosen from historical repeatability data.
- For a returning buyer, do not show the same products they already bought; present a welcome-back message and what to try next based on what they have tried.
- Segment by lifetime value: the source says someone who spends over $500 with them should be treated very differently from someone who has never seen the brand.
- Build the depth of this journey deliberately — the message and product set should change with the customer's stage, not just the acquisition campaign.
Caveat: Requires purchase history and some data depth; the source's $500 threshold is his own brand's example.
Caveat: Works best with products that have continuation or expansion paths; a single-SKU store has limited levers.

Tags: multi, retention, merchandising, customer-research, email-marketing, product-page
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Fix the homepage for your SKU count
Use when: Homepage and landing page design: structuring the first screens of a store based on how many products you sell.
- For low-SKU stores, keep the landing page close to a landing page with a little brand story; the single product should be added to cart or checkout as fast as possible with minimal extra clicks.
- For high-SKU stores, put the current offer or promoted campaign in the header area where it gets the most visibility.
- Directly beneath that, show the highest-AOV bundles and packs — the source points to True Classic's pack structure as an example — acknowledging that raising the first-order value is the goal for every store.
- Further down, introduce categories so shoppers with many SKUs can browse, plus reviews and feedback for individual items.
- Do not overcomplicate the number of pages at the start.
Caveat: The True Classic reference is the source's example of testing volume, not a guarantee your store will match it.
Caveat: High-AOV merchandising assumes your economics and fulfilment can support larger pack sizes.

Tags: multi, merchandising, landing-page, product-page, conversion-optimization, bundles
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Replace blank white PDP first images with lifestyle imagery
Use when: PDP optimisation: revising the first image and adjacent copy on a product page.
- Audit the first image on each product page; if it is a plain product on white, replace it with a lifestyle image, the product in use, or a dynamic shot.
- Put the strongest benefit headlines next to the hero rather than a weak description of why someone would buy.
- Use the first-image choice as a split test to see whether lifestyle context lifts performance versus the plain shot.
- Pair the visual change with the strongest angle discovered in your smoke tests so the PDP matches the ad that brought the visitor.
Caveat: The source allows product-on-white can be a useful A/B variant, but calls it a wasted default, not an absolute requirement in every category.
Caveat: Marketplace conventions (mentioned for Amazon) can differ from DTC norms; match the channel the shopper expects.

Tags: multi, product-page, conversion-optimization, ad-creative, merchandising, experiment-design
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Use clipping marketplaces to scale distribution cheaply
Use when: Acquisition creative sourcing: testing a paid clipper model to add volume and impressions beyond your own accounts.
- Choose an offer and state a budget plus a target CPM (the source's example: $5,000 at an 85-cent to $1 target CPM — a figure to treat as illustrative, not a benchmark).
- Provide the creative brief and assets you want used so the clippers post material consistent with your angles.
- Use the marketplace's approval step: you don't pay until you approve a post.
- Accept the cap: if a clip goes viral and would be worth far more at the target CPM, you still pay only the agreed budget.
- Expect the audience to be random pages driving to your site, which means you need an organised backlog of briefs and assets to keep feeding the army.
- Treat follower counts as irrelevant; the source's framing is that impressions and traffic back to the store are what matter.
Caveat: He predicted the tactic would become widely known and CPMs could rise as large advertisers enter; verify current marketplace terms and pricing before committing.
Caveat: The clip model relies on clippers not needing the physical product, which may not fit every category or legal/compliance context.

Tags: multi, acquisition, creative-strategy, ad-creative, influencer, budgeting, paid-social
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Set up a testing pipeline and organic posting habit
Use when: Standing up a paid social testing process and deciding whether organic posting is worth the time for an ecommerce brand.
- Start the tree with image smoke tests, expand winners into video, then add creators, colours and regions as you learn.
- Alongside the paid tests, post organically on your channels; the source reports that when the brand stops uploading assets to social channels, ad account performance weakens, and that organic content often becomes top-performing paid creative because it doesn't feel like an ad.
- If you don't yet have an ad account, post on every platform as a starting practice — the source suggests twice a day as a best-practice target.
- Route learnings back to creators quickly: share what is working in real time, including failed formats to avoid.
- Use the pipeline to answer micro questions — which value prop, which presenter type, which region — and let answers feed the next round of briefs.
Caveat: The claim that organic activity improves the ad account is the source's reported observation, not a documented mechanism; the twice-a-day cadence is his suggested practice.
Caveat: Ad platform behaviour and current posting tools change — verify current platform guidance before building the calendar.

Tags: multi, experiment-design, creative-strategy, paid-social, organic-social, briefing
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Build an always-on creative bench and 30-day asset runway
Use when: Creative and media planning over a month or quarter: keeping a rotating pipeline rather than scheduling one-off production bursts.
- Assume more creative is better than less: with nothing working you need more anyway, and once something works it tells you what more to make.
- Plan in monthly cycles, rotating in drops, holidays and evergreen angles that historically perform, and keep launching those plus new tests.
- Keep testing while new customers are coming in, so the account doesn't run out of fresh winners.
- Maintain roughly a 30-day runway of assets: you can build many variants off what is working now, but only about a month's worth before trends shift and the assets become obsolete.
- Watch for the account being lopsided: if only a couple of proven ads carry spend and every new ad misses, the account can destabilise and the team may have to pull back the new launches.
Caveat: The 30-day runway is the source's rule of thumb, not a calculated optimum.
Caveat: He also acknowledges days when nothing is taking budget and the right move is to pull back rather than force spend.

Tags: multi, creative-strategy, budgeting, ad-creative, experiment-design, team-design
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Brief editors and designers with references plus brand context
Use when: Creative production and outsourcing: writing briefs for external creative help who understand performance marketing.
- Recognise that performance-aware editors are scarce and that using a generic designer to add badges or sparkle produces incoherent ads.
- Give references explicitly and state this is an example of the outcome you want, then supply what your brand stands for and the assets and value props involved.
- Tell the editor they should adapt the reference to your brand rather than copy it word-for-word or pixel-by-pixel.
- Include examples of things that are working and things that failed, while telling creators to keep their own voice because they know their audience.
- Expect that your own idea of what you want becomes clearer once you receive a first version, so budget for a second or third revision rather than judging the initial brief.
- Source talent where time zones align (the source works with editors in Canada and Latin America for this reason) and verify current rates and platforms.
Caveat: The source says brand owners often can't communicate what they want until they see something — plan for iteration rather than expecting a perfect first cut.
Caveat: Talent-market and time-zone specifics change; verify current arrangements.

Tags: multi, briefing, creative-strategy, team-design, ad-creative
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Learn the ad account yourself before hiring out
Use when: Early paid acquisition: deciding whether to manage ads internally or hand them to an agency or freelancer.
- Run the account yourself at the start, up to about $10k-$30k in monthly spend, so you understand what the eventual manager is doing and can ask better questions.
- At very low spend ($3k-$10k/month), weigh the management fee against test budget: paying someone thousands more may leave too little to learn with, so eat the work yourself.
- Use current tools; the source argues they are sophisticated enough that you don't need heavy outside support.
- If you do want help, hire someone for a short consult or a weekly look over your shoulder rather than a full retainer.
- Insert an outside expert for a limited weekly audit while an internal person learns — the source used this as a hedge during a handover.
Caveat: The $10k-$30k threshold is the source's rule of thumb, not a computed break-even.
Caveat: At higher spend the internal creative-strategist model with a P&L-aware owner becomes more viable than founder operation.

Tags: multi, team-design, paid-social, budgeting, acquisition, measurement
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Track daily burn, discount rate and high-value orders together
Use when: Finance and acquisition coordination: setting daily tracking and deciding when to pull ad spend or run promos.
- Track daily spend and return at the channel level each day — the source's team reviews spend and return hourly, Monday to Sunday.
- Add discount as a percent of sales as a core metric and know your sweet spot; if sales rise while discount percent rises too, you may not be outrunning burn.
- Track orders over $1,000 per day as an indicator of high-value customer activity.
- Use discount dollars as a lever that trades off against ad spend: when media pulls back, promotions or discounts can fill the gap for those days.
- Keep the marketing and finance forecast in the same conversation so spend changes are made with the daily cash position in mind.
Caveat: Hourly, daily, always-on review reflects a brand at the source's scale; smaller brands may track less frequently but should still monitor burn and discount rate together.
Caveat: The $1,000 order threshold is his brand's metric, not a universal target.

Tags: multi, measurement, budgeting, pricing, retention, acquisition
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## PDP hero image: lifestyle over white-background product shot
Use when: Designing or A/B testing the lead image and above-the-fold layout on a product detail page.
- Audit your PDP hero images: if the first thing a shopper sees is a bare product on a white background, flag it for testing.
- Build a lifestyle alternative that shows the product in use, on a person, or in its real context, and test it as the PDP first image against the current shot.
- Recognize that the image sits next to your description: a strong hero image plus weak copy wastes the real estate, so pair the image change with benefit-led headline copy.
- Use Amazon-branded product pages as the reference standard for image density and optimization, since the source argues their traffic volume forces continuous testing of imagery and buy-button placement.
- Treat this as an ongoing split test, not a one-time swap; first-image choice is called out as one of the more important PDP tests.
Caveat: Source praises Amazon-style pages as the most optimized but does not provide a benchmark; your catalog may not support the same image volume.

Tags: multi, product-page, conversion-optimization, experiment-design, merchandising, creative-strategy
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Increase AOV on the PDP with frequently-bought-together blocks
Use when: Merchandising a PDP or cart for a brand with multiple SKUs, packs, or add-on options.
- Identify the SKUs most commonly purchased together or that logically bundle (e.g., a product plus an accessory or different pack size).
- Build a clearly laid-out 'frequently bought together' or bundle module on the PDP and in the cart, making the combined purchase easy to add in one action.
- Design explicit pack ladders (e.g., six-pack vs 12-pack) so shoppers can self-select the larger option when intent is high.
- Consider that the entry pack shapes repeat behavior: the source observed that a larger initial pack drives faster consumption and repeat purchase, so treat pack size as both an AOV and a retention lever.
- Test placement and which bundle sits in the highest-visibility slot.
Caveat: The source's claim that a 12-pack leads to faster repeat purchase is based on their own emerging data at year two; smaller stores may lack enough order history to confirm this pattern.

Tags: multi, product-page, bundles, pricing, conversion-optimization, retention, merchandising
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Strategic homepage offer placement by margin and inventory
Use when: Deciding which product, bundle, or offer to feature in the homepage hero or primary merchandising slot.
- List your current offers and annotate each with its margin and any inventory you need to clear.
- Place the highest-margin offer or the product you are trying to drive through inventory in the most prominent homepage position.
- Define one clear 'big offer' for the homepage rather than diluting attention across many promos.
- Continue down the homepage into category and insight layers so shoppers with many SKUs can browse and find feedback on a specific SKU.
- Align the homepage hero choice with current ad traffic so the landing offer matches the ad's promise.
Caveat: The source is expressing a preference for margin-driven placement; it is a judgment call, not a tested rule with published results.

Tags: multi, merchandising, homepage, pricing, offer-design, conversion-optimization
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Designing acquisition offers for a high-CPM environment
Use when: Building a new-customer acquisition offer when paid media costs are high and first-order economics are tight.
- Define the acquisition offer so it is clearly more valuable than simply landing on the website and is unique to buying direct.
- Identify the single SKU or product that, when bought first, drives the most customer lifetime value, and make that the entry offer.
- Plan the secondary and tertiary products that attach to that first purchase so the offer opens a path to repeat buys (e.g., a consumable plus a low-cost accessory).
- Use the framework of two goals at any time: get existing buyers to spend more, or get more people to spend at all.
- Within those two buckets, check margins to decide which offers you can actually afford to run.
Caveat: The $35–$45 CPM range is the source's own dataset, not a universal benchmark; the source contrasts it with a pre-2020 era of roughly $10–$15 CPMs.

Tags: multi, offer-design, acquisition, pricing, customer-lifetime-value, creative-strategy
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Use high-perceived-value, low-COGS gifts with purchase instead of discounts
Use when: Deciding how to incentivize a first purchase or subscription while protecting margin.
- Pick a GWP item with high perceived value but low cost of goods (the source uses the example of a towel, scrunchie, cup, mug, or blender).
- Run the arbitrage math: if the item's cost is $100 and it reduces CAC by more than $100, the GWP pays for itself, especially when back-end LTV is strong.
- If the GWP mainly makes customers stickier rather than lowering CAC, you can still justify it by baking the cost into front-end acquisition and winning on the back end.
- Use GWP-style offers to create different entry points into the brand beyond discounts, which the source argues are the primary lever for new customer acquisition as ad costs rise.
- Consider giving a new product free to existing subscribers as a low-cost way to increase perceived value.
Caveat: This is the source's stated framework for deciding, not a measured result; GWP effectiveness depends on your COGS and CAC, and may be less effective than a discount in some categories.

Tags: multi, offer-design, gifts-with-purchase, acquisition, pricing, retention
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Organize offer testing by traffic source and margin
Use when: Building a repeatable offer-testing calendar rather than improvising promos.
- Segment offers by traffic source (e.g., app, Google, Meta, Twitter, direct mail) because a customer from each channel carries a different expected value based on how long they stay and spend.
- Collect the data needed to compare channel-level customer value before committing to channel-specific offers.
- For each offer, ask whether the goal is to make existing customers spend more or to increase the number of people who spend.
- Screen each idea against margin: can you afford this offer at all?
- Set an operating cadence for how many unique offers go live per quarter; the source set a KPI of 15 unique offers in one quarter once the team was in place.
Caveat: The 15-offers-per-quarter target is a source-specific KPI from their team capacity, not a recommended universal number.
Caveat: Channel-level customer value requires enough data volume to be meaningful.

Tags: multi, offer-design, experiment-design, measurement, acquisition, pricing
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## A basic CRO and customer-data stack for a DTC store
Use when: Choosing tools to support conversion optimization and first-party data collection on a Shopify-style store.
- Use a site-speed tool to monitor and improve load performance (the source cites Nostra, also used for first-party data).
- Add a customer-identification layer to enrich email campaigns (the source was trialing customers.ai for user identification).
- Install a heatmap and customer-experience tracking tool to see on-page behavior (the source cites heatmap.com).
- Use a visual page builder to create custom landing and PDP pages without full dev cycles (the source was on Replo).
- Verify current capabilities and pricing for each tool directly with the vendor, since interfaces and features change.
Caveat: This is one brand's stack at a point in time; tool fit depends on platform, volume, and budget, and capabilities may have changed.

Tags: multi, conversion-optimization, measurement, customer-research, shopify, tools
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Design mobile-first and account for dark mode
Use when: Designing PDPs, landing pages, and email templates for a store whose traffic is majority mobile.
- Check your analytics for the mobile/desktop split; the source found roughly 75% of traffic was mobile after initially optimizing for desktop.
- Design layouts, CTAs, and page structure mobile-first, then adapt upward to desktop.
- Account for dark mode in email and on-site viewing: logos, text, and images should remain legible on dark backgrounds.
- Test the ad and landing experience on mobile as the primary path rather than treating it as a secondary adaptation.
- Optimize both experiences but let mobile drive the design decisions.
Caveat: The ~75% mobile figure is the source's own traffic mix, not a general benchmark; verify your own split.

Tags: multi, conversion-optimization, mobile, email, landing-page, measurement
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Judge email performance by revenue per recipient within segments
Use when: Reporting on email/SMS performance and deciding which segments to prioritize or suppress.
- Calculate revenue per recipient as total revenue divided by recipients, ideally per campaign and per segment.
- Segment the list into buckets such as subscribers, repeat buyers (non-subscription), one-time buyers, and non-buyers, and compute RPR for each.
- The source's subscriber segment returned roughly $8 RPR out of a 323,000-person list, while non-purchasers returned significantly less; treat the subscriber segment as the priority audience for reporting.
- Go deeper by purchase behavior, e.g., six-pack vs 12-pack vs bundle buyers, to see which cohorts are most valuable.
- Use this to suppress or deprioritize low-value groups, e.g., customers who only ever buy on discount; the source suggests suppressing them entirely rather than repeatedly paying to reach them.
- Export customer-level purchase history and use AI or spreadsheet analysis to estimate long-term customer value over defined time windows.
Caveat: RPR values are specific to the source's list and cohort definitions; the $8 figure is an example, not a benchmark.
Caveat: Customer-level analysis requires exporting and joining order data, which the source calls more difficult than campaign-level RPR.

Tags: multi, retention, measurement, email, customer-research, segmentation
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Map subscription churn peaks and intercept them
Use when: Reducing subscription churn and building the post-purchase communications calendar.
- Expect a large day-one cancellation spike from customers who subscribed only for the discount; the source notes these customers were likely never going to stay, and this spike heavily skews overall churn numbers.
- Counter it in the first seven days with communication: tell them what to expect, the feeling/effect, quality, product-use cases, and how to consume it, plus customer reviews.
- Anticipate a second peak around day 28 when the billing reminder triggers, and a third in the roughly day 31–45 window; plan messages before each.
- Use subscriber-only giveaways that cost little, e.g., entering anyone subscribed past the 27th into a draw for more of the product they already subscribe to.
- Make it easy to cancel; the source notes forced minimum subscription terms are no longer legally viable and argues you should give people a fast off-ramp instead.
- Track churn by period: the source moved from 24% churn in Q4 to 17% by focusing on this, with a stated goal of sub-5% aggregate churn.
Caveat: The 24%→17% and sub-5% figures are the source's own numbers and goals; churn rates vary widely by category and price point.
Caveat: Reducing churn is described as more product-dependent than tactic-dependent at their stage.

Tags: multi, retention, subscriptions, churn, email, measurement
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Pre-empt the four stated cancellation reasons with downgrades and alternatives
Use when: Designing cancellation flows and retention offers for subscription or repeat-purchase products.
- Recognize the four reasons the source hears on cancellation: can't afford it, have too much product, the effect isn't what they wanted, or found another brand.
- For 'too much product,' offer education on alternate uses (e.g., mocktail recipes, giving it to a friend) and offer to downgrade: 12-pack to six-pack, or a smaller format with fewer milligrams or fewer cans.
- Where users want control, offer a self-dosing format so they can make the product into whatever drink they want.
- For 'too expensive,' treat price as the likely root cause and consider discounts or incentives rather than just product changes.
- For 'effect isn't what I wanted,' focus on usage education and expectation-setting in earlier onboarding.
- Build these as selectable paths in the cancellation flow so the reason routes to the right save action.
Caveat: The four reasons are what customers told the source; your cancellation reasons may differ, so collect your own verbatim data first.

Tags: multi, retention, subscriptions, churn, customer-research, offer-design
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Send plain-text founder and team emails to build retention
Use when: Planning the monthly retention email calendar and deciding what non-promotional content to send.
- Send plain-text emails with no graphics from the founder, from customer support, and from product development on a roughly monthly cadence.
- Use them for product education: step-by-step guidance on exactly how and when to use the product for maximum output, which the source says is under-taught.
- Use them for non-revenue communication: the source cites an email teasing a launch and a livestream that generated about $40,000 with nothing purchasable except a footer link.
- For smaller brands, lean into being the underdog and tell people you are a small business that appreciates their business; the source notes this works better before scale.
- Time plain-text sends to relevant moments, such as price changes or tariff-related news, using playful, honest framing.
- Segment by cohort so the copy speaks natively to the specific customer.
Caveat: The $40,000 email result is a single example, not a promise.
Caveat: Founder-voice messages lose effectiveness at scale, per the source.

Tags: multi, retention, email, lifecycle-marketing, copywriting, segmentation
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Run response-driven campaigns to improve deliverability and engagement
Use when: Trying to lift email engagement or sender reputation, or needing user-generated content for retention and social.
- Diagnose the goal: the source ran a themed campaign because spam/deliverability was a problem and they needed mass replies, since replies are one of the few ways to prompt action.
- Create a simple participation mechanic tied to a cultural moment.
- Run it for a full month, collecting submissions and having the team rate/score them, then communicate back what people sent and what can be made with the product.
- Feed the resulting user content back into emails and social.
- Incentivize reflection on the product: invite customers to submit an image of the product or how they use it.
Caveat: The source links the campaign to improved response rate but gives no numeric benchmark, and reply-based deliverability effects vary by list and provider.

Tags: multi, retention, email, deliverability, user-generated-content, customer-research
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

## Turn loyal customers into marketers with one-person asks
Use when: Building referral and word-of-mouth programs for repeat buyers.
- Identify your highest-value customer cohort and speak with them directly where feasible; the source used to personally call top customers weekly.
- Ask each customer to tell exactly one person—not five—because a one-person ask is achievable and more likely to be done.
- Personalize the request by calling out that the referred person is a friend of theirs so they are motivated to make it a good experience.
- Leverage existing distribution: if you have a large social following, offer co-branded posts with influencers and creators, trading brand distribution for better rates and stronger partnerships.
- Recognize that a referred customer avoids acquisition cost, which the source calls game-changing for unit economics.
Caveat: The one-person ask and weekly calls are the source's practices, not tested benchmarks; do not assume a specific referral rate.

Tags: multi, retention, acquisition, referral, influencer, community
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Fund a surprise-and-delight budget at the CX layer
Use when: Setting customer service policy and deciding how to handle damaged, missing, or unsatisfactory orders.
- Separate budgets: keep a discount budget and a separate surprise-and-delight ('wow') budget that the CX team can use at its discretion.
- When an order arrives damaged or crushed, replace it generously (the source sends back a six-pack) and tell the customer to keep or give away the original.
- For problems, over-deliver relative to the complaint; the source argues that net of true COGS, the extra goodwill revenue from a large order or word of mouth usually exceeds the give-away cost.
- Treat the wow moment as a trigger for word of mouth, especially when the product is displayed in the customer's home or expresses their identity.
- Attach a dedicated person to own this and respond across channels: the source hired a head of customer engagement to handle the wow budget and answer every comment and DM across seven channels daily.
Caveat: The source's cost-justification is a judgment based on product COGS and perceived value; it may not hold for low-margin or low-visibility products.

Tags: multi, retention, customer-service, word-of-mouth, community, margin
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Product selection: require repeat purchase, an emotional effect, and efficient packaging
Use when: Evaluating new product lines or SKUs for an ecommerce catalog.
- Prioritize products that facilitate a personal, repeatable experience: the source cites hydration/electrolyte packets and fragrance as categories where the customer buys again because they feel the effect.
- Favor categories with repeat consumability so each purchase reopens the acquisition window.
- Design the item to ship in a small parcel that fits a sleeve or can be fulfilled at volume; avoid large or bulky formats that inflate shipping cost and EBIDTA impact.
- Bring in packaging/logistics expertise early to engineer the parcel size, as the source cites Native engaging a shipping specialist up front and describes cents-per-unit savings compounding into large annual figures.
- Watch input costs (plastics, cardboard, aluminum) and tariffs, since material costs and packaging changes affect unit economics.
- If a packaging change costs slightly more but reduces breakage, run the net math: the source changed cans because too many were crushing.
Caveat: The $17-cent-per-unit and $8-million examples are the source's own figures from their operations, not a general benchmark.

Tags: multi, product-selection, fulfillment, pricing, margin, operations
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Product expansion: compete on format and effect, not just flavor
Use when: Planning a product-line expansion or deciding how to position new SKUs on shelf and online.
- Assess the shelf at retail: the source observes products are typically merchandised in threes (e.g., an original, a variant, and a flavor).
- Choose a differentiation axis other than flavor count, such as effects (energetic vs relaxing) or dayparts (morning vs night, going out vs winding down).
- Walk your own category's retail shelf and analyze how the products marry together and how many facings fit on the shelf; the source describes this exercise as very useful before expanding.
- Match the product experience to the occasion the customer wants it for, rather than adding undifferentiated SKUs.
- Bring in a formulator and a retail veteran to pressure-test the expansion roadmap and shelf realities.
Caveat: The shelf-in-threes observation is a general pattern the source noticed, not a rule.

Tags: multi, product-selection, merchandising, positioning, retail, category-research
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

---

## Build product feedback loops with post-purchase surveys and reviews
Use when: Designing a process to feed customer data into product development, marketing, and sales outreach.
- Send a post-purchase survey asking how they heard about you, what they expect from the product, and where they expect to use it.
- Treat the 'how did you hear about us' answer as a last-touch attribution signal, since customers reliably recall what they touched last even if multi-touch attribution is noisy; the source argues this should be treated as law and piped into Slack (an easy Zapier integration).
- Trigger automated review requests when the product arrives, so positive reviews come in quickly.
- Use a positive review plus a repeat-purchase signal to trigger a subscription offer at a better discount.
- Flag unusually large orders (e.g., 48+ or 64 cases) so sales or community teams can follow up on what event or use case is driving the purchase.
- Layer cohorts for feedback collection: first-time purchasers, repeat purchasers, and non-purchasers all have different experiences to mine.
Caveat: Self-reported attribution is anecdotal and can be inaccurate; the source treats it as a directional signal alongside more rigorous measurement.

Tags: multi, customer-research, attribution, post-purchase, email, automation
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

## Weigh building in public against key-man risk and stop-start effects
Use when: Deciding whether the founder or brand should publicly share metrics, revenue, and process content as part of acquisition and brand strategy.
- Map your brand-building approach: some brands (cited: Represent, Minted New York, Cadence) share product development and story rather than granular financials, which the source calls comparatively safe.
- If you share numbers, count the benefits: signaling to the market (investors, acquirers, competitors, potential employees), attracting retail partners, and trading distribution for better tech and partnership terms.
- Account for the cost: the source reports disproportionate advantage while posting consistently, but a drop in CAC benefit if you stop, and describes stopping during COVID-era interruption as having an effect.
- Recognize key-man risk: if the public face of the brand stops posting or changes their presented persona, the source argues the brand can suffer; make the public-building plan feasible long-term and build a real moat.
- Broaden participation by having more of the team share the spotlight so the story does not depend on one person.
- The source, having built this way, says if starting over they would not go as deep publicly, though they still see the reach as worth it.
Caveat: The CAC-lowering and door-opening benefits are the source's own experience, not measured benchmarks.
Caveat: This is presented as a double-edged sword; the source explicitly says they would dial it back if starting again.

Tags: multi, brand-building, acquisition, content-strategy, founder-brand, risk
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

## Build a personal content system: pillars, weekly debrief, no AI voice
Use when: Planning a founder-led content or social calendar that supports an ecommerce brand's acquisition.
- Define a small number of content pillars: the source uses the brand, the agency/learnings (paid media, email, SMS, creative), and personal life and family.
- Hold a weekly one-to-two-hour debrief to verbally brainstorm topics that are timely or personally important, then have writers turn those into drafts in your own voice.
- Keep the copy human-written; the source's only AI use is analyzing which past posts performed organically, then reworking a strong performer into a new format (e.g., tweet to graphic).
- Maintain a running Google Doc of current interests and projects that you update every couple of weeks as the topic source.
- Use a project/projection/reflection rhythm: talk about what you are going to do that week, then report back on what happened and what you learned.
- If budget is limited, use scheduling/writing tools and a trending-post discovery tool for inspiration, and study a low-cost solo-entrepreneur content course to understand paid/organic principles (verify current tool names and pricing, as they change).
Caveat: The source credits a specific low-priced LinkedIn course and creator; no results are given for that course, and tooling pricing and features change over time.

Tags: multi, content-strategy, founder-brand, acquisition, tools, scheduling
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

## Route acquisition and spend decisions through people with media-buying experience
Use when: Deciding who should own paid acquisition, or whether to build a brand versus run media buying as a service.
- Recognize that a strong media buyer is someone who can spend aggressively without being emotionally tied to each dollar; founders spending their own money often struggle with this.
- If you are a product person without acquisition skill, you become dependent on others for growth decisions; the source argues you need enough paid-media literacy to know what a good marketer looks like.
- Consider that agency and performance backgrounds make good founders or co-founders for brands, since they bring tested growth knowledge and spend discipline.
- When evaluating a rollup or portfolio strategy, avoid a single centralized CMO across brands that target different customers; the source cites this as the core mistake of certain ecommerce rollup models.
- If your product category has high barriers to entry (e.g., regulation or specialized marketing knowledge), expect fewer but larger competitors and plan accordingly.
- The source's view is that whoever can spend the most wins at scale, so control of acquisition capability is a strategic asset.
Caveat: The claim that 'he who can spend the most wins' is the source's opinion, not an established rule, and it ignores creative and product differentiation.

Tags: multi, acquisition, agency, media-buying, positioning, strategy
Source: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx
